entries.title: Luis Castillo gives White Sox just what they want in first home start
entries.summary: <p>That was the Luis Castillo the White Sox were hoping for.</p><p>Castillo, the 10-year veteran acquired from the Mariners two days before the trade deadline, pitched seven scoreless innings Wednesday against the Reds, allowing one hit and two walks in his first home start at Rate Field. He set a season high with 10 strikeouts.</p><p>Manager Will Venable is looking for length from Castillo to help a rotation that largely has been short on it. He got that and more as Castillo rebounded from his Sox debut, in which he allowed five runs in four innings last Thursday in Boston.</p><p>“That was awesome. In control the whole time,” Venable said. “He attacked the zone really well. He and Drew Romo were on the same page. Drew did an outstanding job; another shutout that he’s caught for us. [Castillo] didn’t let them get anything going.”</p><p>Romo also provided a rare boost with his bat, hitting his first home run since May 25, a 403-foot solo shot. Chase Meidroth, back from a two-game break to nurse a sore left wrist, hit a two-run homer, and Munetaka Murakami walked to extend his on-base streak to 27 games.</p><p>“I’ve been trying a lot of stuff in the cage,” said Romo, who entered the game hitting .126. “Everything is good in the cage, and then I go out on the field, and it goes back to the way it was. So I’m like, I’m just not going to hit today. And then I went and did that. So I guess I’m not going to hit again.”</p><p>Castillo retired 11 consecutive batters between his walks and fanned the final four batters he faced. Never mind that Reds hitters had the third-most strikeouts and the worst batting average in the majors at the time of his departure. They never even reached second base.</p><p>At 89 pitches after six innings, Castillo had every intention of pitching the seventh.</p><p>“After the sixth, [Venable] came to me and asked if I wanted one more inning,” said Castillo, who threw 105 pitches. “I said, ‘Yeah, of course.’ I was looking at him like, what are you talking about? I really wanted that seventh.”</p><h3>Lineup shuffle</h3><p>Thinking of the big picture as the Sox pursue a playoff spot, Venable gave third baseman Miguel Vargas the day off.</p><p>“I know we just had an off day [Monday], but to get a couple of these guys a couple days off here as we get into this stretch,” Venable said of the Sox’ 16 games in 16 days. “It might just be one more for some of these guys in September. Got a long way to go here.”</p><p>With Vargas out of the lineup, Venable put Colson Montgomery at third base, Meidroth at shortstop and Sam Antonacci at second. That opened up left field for Tristan Peters and center for Brenton Doyle, who earned high praise from Venable.</p><p>“He’s solid in his swing decisions,” Venable said. “He’s got power, he’s hitting the ball hard, he’s an elite defender, he runs the bases well. You just look at him physically and like having that on the field. He’s great in the clubhouse. He’s checking all the boxes for us. The more we can expose him to the field, the better for us.”</p><h3>Colson’s bad timing</h3><p>Montgomery continues to search for his stroke at the plate. In four at-bats, he struck out looking, popped out, lined a single to right at almost 114 mph and walked. Venable said the problem is Montgomery’s timing.</p><p>“It has been inconsistency with his timing at the plate,” he said. “Saw him tap into it the other day, hits that homer; it’s just been inconsistent. For him to put himself in a position to see the ball, make good swing decisions and get good swings off, it’s really important to have his timing. And when it’s not there, that’s when you see the inconsistency in the swings, in the contact.”</p><h3>‘What an at-bat’</h3><p>Reds reliever Emilio Pagan won a 14-pitch battle against Antonacci on Tuesday, striking him out with the tying run on second in the 10th inning. He was complimentary of the Sox rookie.</p><p>“What an at-bat by him,” said Pagan, a 10-year veteran. “I threw some really good pitches up and away, which is my go-to whiff pitch. Got the breaking ball in on him; he fouled that off, too. Laid off a split off the plate. entries.title: Alex Bregman hits three homers as title-chasing Cubs follow ring-winners’ example: ‘They lead by action’
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON – The way <b>Alex Bregman</b>’s season has gone, each productive day at the plate is cautiously described as “a step in the right direction.”</p><p>Those steps are adding up, none more “right” than the three-homer, seven-RBI game he had in Wednesday’s 12-6 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> win over the Nationals.</p><p>We’ve wondered plenty of times whether Bregman was finally back, but after smacking four homers and driving in eight runs in the first two games of this series, maybe Bregman is finally back.</p><p>In his last 26 games, Bregman is batting .306, with nine homers, nine doubles, 26 RBIs, a .397 on-base percentage and a 1.054 OPS.</p><p>“The last month or so has been a step in the right direction, but really, the last two days have been a real step in the right direction,” Bregman said, offering a glimpse into his much-discussed off-field work. “I’ve had days this year when it’s gone all right, I had a few extra-base hits, and then the next day, you wake up and you get to the ballpark and it feels completely different</p><p>“We went through the archives for this, like way back in the day, all the changes … throughout my career. We were watching Corpus Christi Double-A video two nights ago in my room at 1 o’clock.”</p><p>The on-field production is starting to catch up with the impact the two-time World Series champ has made <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/07/cubs-alex-bregman-home-run-ryan-zeferjahn-bullpen-pitcher-mlb-trade-deadline-angels" >helping teammates behind the scenes</a>.</p><p>“[That part of his] personality really fit in seamlessly,” said shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson</b>, who also homered in Wednesday’s win. “The one thing he’s brought so much is being able to help guys navigate through things, whether it’s other guys and their at-bats, pitchers and their approach to getting other teams out.</p><p>“He’s best when he’s got his hands in everything.”</p><p>As the Cubs chase a championship, guys with rings like Bregman and Swanson are models for their title-hungry teammates.</p><p>“Just being able to talk to guys like Bregman and Dansby, who have won World Series,” lefty reliever <b>Ryan Rolison</b> said Wednesday, “it’s super special and fun every day to come to work.</p><p>“They lead by action. You can see the way they navigate through the ups and downs. Both of them have had ups and downs this year, and there’s no panic. The numbers at the end of the year are going to be where they are [supposed to be].</p><p>“Those guys are established big league players, and being able to see their work ethic day in and day out and the mindset they bring every single day? You have a bad day at the field, flush it, it’s a new day the next day.”</p><p><b>Maton’s knee</b></p><p>Righty reliever <b>Phil Maton</b>, signed to be a key bullpen piece, has been on the injured list since July 20, dealing with a knee injury that’s landed him there three times this season.</p><p>The next couple weeks will be critical in determining if Maton, who owns a 6.18 ERA, will pitch again this season.</p><p>“We’re trying to figure out, ‘Where are you at with your knee?’ And then we’ve got to make a decision as to, ‘Can you get back, or does this make sense to even try?’” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “If he can pitch, he’s going to pitch. But are we putting off something that’s going to keep happening?</p><p>“That’s what we have to make a final decision on and Phil has to make a decision on shortly.”</p><p><b>Local product</b></p><p>The Cubs faced Nationals lefty <b>Jackson Kent</b> on Wednesday, a Chicagoland native and Lake Park High School alum who struck out six in his major league debut.</p>

entries.title: Sky coach Tyler Marsh voices support for Stephanie White amid right-wing outrage
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — The fallout from DiJonai Carrington’s flagrant foul on Fever guard Sophie Cunningham keeps echoing. In the latest development, Fever coach Stephanie White has become public enemy No. 1 in some corners of Indiana.</p><p>Fans booed her during the Fever’s most recent home game. The lieutenant governor called for her firing.</p><p>All because White said after the Sky game that she didn’t believe Carrington’s foul was intentional — and made clear that she knows Carrington, whom she coached in Connecticut, as a player who always plays hard and doesn’t give up open layups.</p><p>“No solid coach would ever take the side of the opposing team’s player who committed a flagrant foul on one of your own players,” Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith posted on X. “Terrible coaching! The Fever need to defend their players.”</p><p>White <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/11/indiana-fever-coach-stephanie-white-dijonai-carrington-sophie-cunningham" >responded</a> before Tuesday’s game against New York, warning that hate and fearmongering were threatening to hijack the league. She also said she took personally the suggestion that she doesn’t defend her players.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/11/indiana-fever-coach-stephanie-white-dijonai-carrington-sophie-cunningham" >Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White says divisiveness ‘will not win’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/10/dijonai-carrington-says-white-privilege-post-goes-beyond-flagrant-foul" >DiJonai Carrington says ‘WHITE PRIVILEGE’ post goes beyond flagrant foul</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“For those who have anything to say about the play in the last game: I didn't see the play in real time,” White said. “Thankfully Sophie's OK. Was it egregious? Absolutely. When you have a chance to watch that over and over on replay, you can see that.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> coach Tyler Marsh, no stranger to scrutiny himself, sympathized with White and the challenge of keeping outside noise from shaping how a coach operates.</p><p>“At the end of the day, she’s trying to look out for her players, and every coach can respect that,” Marsh said. “I’m not sure that there’s any two teams in this league as heavily scrutinized as us.”</p><p>Despite the Fever’s 21-12 record and White’s previous success with the Sun, she has dealt with loud criticism all season.</p><p>Earlier this year, a video of White subbing Caitlin Clark out of a huddle because of her defense went viral. A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/09/the-wnbas-gratitude-police-have-a-blind-spot-for-fevers-sophie-cunningham" >familiar online conclusion </a>followed: White wasn’t properly grateful for Clark.</p><p>Her players, however, don’t appear to share the outrage. Clark said the booing from fans made her sick. Cunningham said White had her back, and even called Carrington a “hell of a player.”</p><p>White had another backer Wednesday in one of her former players, Sky guard Rachel Banham.</p><p>“She’s such a good person, such a great coach,” Banham said. “She really does love her players. She means that when she says that.</p><p>“She coached Nai. She knows exactly how Nai plays. She wasn’t saying that to not defend Sophie by any means. She agreed that it was an ‘egregious’ foul. She loves her Indy girls. She’ll ride for them as hard as she can.</p><p>“But she’s still gonna be honest and know that Nai’s trying to throw that thing off the backboard, and she missed, and they called the flagrant, and that’s what it is.”</p><p>Carrington <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/10/dijonai-carrington-says-white-privilege-post-goes-beyond-flagrant-foul" >said Sunday</a> that her foul on Cunningham was not intentional. She said she had spoken to the league about her post in which she wrote “WHITE PRIVILEGE” and tagged the Fever, which she said went beyond the ejection itself.</p><p>She said Wednesday that she had no additional comment on the matter.</p><p>Marsh, meanwhile, has continued to support Carrington. Before the Sky’s game against the Valkyries on Wednesday, he said the uproar hasn’t become a distraction in the locker room.</p><p>“We rally around her,” he said. “She’s a hard-nosed, passionate player. She cares for her teammates, and her teammates feel the same way about her. We keep it moving as best we can.”</p><p>At some point the rest of the world might decide to keep it moving, too.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: WNBA denounces 'bad-faith' transgender debate
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba" >WNBA</a> on Wednesday criticized those trying to create a narrative about transgender women playing in the league.</p><p>"There are no immediate eligibility matters affecting the WNBA, and we strongly denounce the bad-faith efforts to use these topics to demean or marginalize others," a league spokesperson said Wednesday in a statement, hours after an anti-hate task force met virtually and discussed a variety of topics, including social media vitriol and transgender athletes.</p><p>The league's collective bargaining agreement states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA," but it does not include any more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth. Last Friday, two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, declared themselves eligible for the WNBA Draft, saying they identify as women.</p><p>The draft isn't until next April.</p><p>There has never been a transgender woman — a person assigned male at birth who transitions to align with their gender identity — on a WNBA roster. There have been players in the league who were assigned female at birth and later came out as transgender or nonbinary.</p><p>The anti-hate committee was formed last year to deal with hateful and abusive online comments directed at players and the league.</p><p>"Today's meeting covered a wide range of topics, including ongoing discussions on transgender athletes and the continued hate and vitriol directed at players online," the WNBA statement said. "We will continue to engage all league stakeholders in the coming weeks and months. We will approach these important conversations thoughtfully and in alignment with the values of our league."</p><p>WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert sent a memo last Friday to team presidents and general managers saying the league would discuss the subject of transgender women in women's basketball.</p><p>"We recognize that this is a complex and nuanced topic, and we will continue to have important conversations with all of you and the Players Association in the weeks and months ahead," Engelbert said in the memo. "We also plan to convene additional discussions and offer listening sessions for any team leaders who would like to participate. Your perspectives and feedback are invaluable, and I appreciate those who have already reached out to share their thoughts."</p><p>In an ESPN article published last month, Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham voiced support for barring transgender girls and women from girls' and women's sports. Cunningham's comments sparked small rallies and protests <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/08/sophie-cunningham-draws-dueling-protests-outside-sky-fever-game" target="_blank" >at the United Center</a>and in Seattle and Portland when the Fever were on the road last week.</p><p>Some WNBA players and coaches have come out in support of transgender athletes, including Seattle Storm center Stefanie Dolson and Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve.</p><p>"We need to protect trans kids," Reeve said on Aug. 1. "To me, it's a human rights issue. Every kid has a right to sports."</p><p>Many players have declined to comment on the subject.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: White Sox retired Ozzie Guillen's number, sure, but they could've had all-time great Terry Francona — twice
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> made the right managerial hire in November 2003.</p><p>Right for them. Right for the Red Sox — and the Cubs — too.</p><p>Let’s go back so we can tie all this together.</p><p>As that year’s World Series between the Yankees and Marlins was underway, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/08/white-sox-officially-retire-ozzie-guillens-number" target="_blank" >Ozzie Guillen</a>, then the Marlins’ third-base coach, was described by the Sun-Times’ Chris De Luca as “bursting with confidence” before his interview with the White Sox’ then-general manager, Kenny Williams. But Guillen was regarded in the media as a long shot to succeed Jerry Manuel. Two-time World Series winner Cito Gaston seemed a far likelier target, though the tight-fisted Sox would have to pony up to get him. A short list of others — including A’s bench coach Terry Francona, an ex-Phillies skipper who’d managed in the Sox organization, famously having Michael Jordan in Double-A — were widely reported to still be under consideration.</p><p>Guillen, 39, impressed Williams and chairman Jerry Reinsdorf with bold talk about igniting a stagnant Sox clubhouse and got the job. Francona, 45, hadn’t “[made] the earth move,” according to a Sun-Times story. A month later, though, the baby-faced GM of the Red Sox — a not-yet-30 Theo Epstein — made the offer that would put Francona on a path to the Hall of Fame.</p><p>In 2004, Francona’s first season in Boston, the Red Sox ended the Curse of the Bambino, an 86-year championship drought. One year later, Guillen and the White Sox ended an 88-year drought, sweeping the Red Sox in the divisional round along the way. The Red Sox won the World Series again in 2007, making Francona a superstar and Epstein something akin to a superhero. The Cubs eventually threw themselves at Epstein, who was ready for a new challenge heading into 2012, and the mother of all droughts — 108 years — would end in 2016 in Game 7 against Cleveland, which, of course, by then was being managed by Francona.</p><p>See how it all fits? It’s a baseball story that might as well be an anthology film.</p><p>“Wow, [the White Sox] picked me in front of Francona? WOWWW. I’m very pleased they picked me. That’s a privilege for me,” Guillen told me Wednesday.</p><p>According to Francona, in town with his current team, the Reds, to face the White Sox, he wasn’t formally interviewed by the Sox before the job went to Guillen. But he did get an interview heading into 2012, when he was there for the hiring but the Sox instead opted for managerial greenhorn Robin Ventura.</p><p>“I talked to Kenny Williams, it was very quick and I knew I wasn’t getting it,” Francona said. “But I guess I technically interviewed, kind of met him at the airport restaurant and had lunch. That was the extent of it.”</p><p>Who knows? Maybe Reinsdorf will engineer a run at Francona, as he did with Tony La Russa, to manage the Sox when this young core is ready to make a real run at the World Series. You know, a “sorry, Will Venable, for the Ricky Renteria treatment” kind of thing. Probably not. But Francona, 67, has only one guaranteed year left on his Reds contract.</p><p>Francona’s body of work is extraordinary. He entered Wednesday in 11th place on the all-time wins list, with 2,090. The only non-Hall of Fame managers in front of him, Dusty Baker and Bruce Bochy, each will soon be in Cooperstown. Francona is the active leader with more than twice as many wins as A.J. Hinch or Dave Roberts, the next two on the list. Assuming he’s back for a full 2027 season, Francona will pass Joe McCarthy (2,125) and Bucky Harris (2,158) and have a real chance to overtake Baker (2,183) and Sparky Anderson (2,194), putting him in seventh place. If he and the Reds agree on the team’s option for 2028, Francona could pass Bochy (2,252) as well.</p><p>Yep, the Sox — twice — could have had that guy. We haven’t even mentioned that in Francona’s 11 seasons in Cleveland, the last of which was 2023, his teams won four division titles, posted nine winning records and finished below the Sox in the standings a grand total of once.</p><p>“He’s one of the best, period,” Guillen said. “He’s a winner. He gets along with his players very well. That’s the most important thing — he is great and he is still the same guy no matter who you are. He knows he is a Hall of Famer and is a very humble man.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Jerry Reinsdorf and Michael Jordan’s old manager catch up during BP. <a href="https://t.co/4tnNJG4w1z">pic.twitter.com/4tnNJG4w1z</a></p>— Gordon Wittenmyer (@GDubMLB) <a href="https://x.com/GDubMLB/status/2087301157060583500?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Not that the Sox regret going with Guillen, whose No. 13 was just retired at Rate Field last weekend. Guillen is 97th on the wins list (747), though he is the first Ozzie.</p><p>“I thought he was good for the game,” Francona said of Guillen. “He certainly wasn’t boring. And when we first came here, man, they played kind of like his personality. They had some pretty good teams.”</p><p>But what if? Francona instead of Guillen way back when would’ve been interesting.</p><p>“I [would have stayed with] the Marlins and I know I would have been managing that team,” Guillen said.</p><p>And how would that have gone?</p><p>Said Guillen: “My career never [would have been] the same.”</p><p>How true that is.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/02/18/reds-terry-francona-elly-de-la-cruz-hunter-greene-cubs-mlb-national-league-central" >Reds’ Terry Francona — best manager in the NL Central? — taking aim at Cubs, division crown</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/08/white-sox-officially-retire-ozzie-guillens-number" target="_blank" >White Sox officially retire Ozzie Guillen’s No. 13</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: With playoff chances dwindling, time for Sky fans to look to the future
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — With 11 games left in the season, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> are still motivated by the possibility of making the playoffs, however remote it has become. ESPN’s model gives them just <a class="Link" href="https://www.espn.com/wnba/bpi/_/view/playoffs" target="_blank" >a 0.1% chance.</a> They would have to go undefeated, or close to it, while also getting an inexplicable collapse from the teams occupying the final playoff spots: the Wings, Liberty and Mystics.</p><p>So for everyone outside the locker room, the focus can start turning toward the future, which hinges on a few big questions.</p><h3><b>How good is the Sky’s young core, really?</b></h3><p></p><p>When general managers voted on the league’s best young cores in the preseason, the Sky were nowhere to be found. For much of the season, that seemed justified. Unlike the Storm, Mystics and Wings, they still don’t have an All-Star in their mix.</p><p>But they do have some sleepers. Before tearing her ACL, Rickea Jackson was averaging 22 points per game. Rookie Sydney Taylor has exploded onto the scene as an elite shot creator. And while Kamilla Cardoso’s season hasn’t been the flashiest, she has evolved into the kind of paint presence opponents have to worry about every night.</p><p>That gives the Sky a legitimate foundation. If Gabriela Jaquez, Jacy Sheldon and Aicha Coulibaly can take meaningful steps forward, the picture starts looking considerably better.</p><h3><b>What can they get out of their draft capital?</b></h3><p>Given the current standings, the Sky are likely to own the Nos. 10 and 11 picks in the 2027 draft through the Mystics and Dream.</p><p>The last time they picked at Nos. 10 and 11, in 2025, they came away with Hailey Van Lith, who didn’t stick, and Ajša Sivka, an international prospect who unexpectedly chose to return to college.</p><p>They’ll need to do better this time. Especially because of what they’re sending out the door.</p><p>The Sky are on track to send a lottery pick — currently carrying the second-best odds at the No. 1 selection — to the Mystics. That could mean waving goodbye to a chance at college phenoms such as JuJu Watkins, Madison Booker or Hannah Hidalgo, any of whom could develop into a superstar. Not something fans will easily forget.</p><h3><b>How will they solve their point guard puzzle?</b></h3><p>The Sky entered the season with three veteran point guards in Skylar Diggins, Courtney Vandersloot and Natasha Cloud — and the fit became predictably messy.</p><p>Diggins hasn’t played since early July, when she posted on social media after being benched and expressed disappointment with her experience in Chicago. She has since been rehabbing a knee injury and did not travel with the team to the West Coast.</p><p>The offseason could give Diggins time to get healthy and the two sides a chance to smooth things over. Or, with Diggins under contract through 2027, the Sky could try to find a trade partner.</p><p>Then there’s Cloud. Like Vandersloot, she has put together a solid 10-point, five-assist season, and quickly became the heart of the locker room. Reason enough to resign her.</p><p>But there’s also an argument for getting younger at the position and finding someone who can develop under Vandersloot rather than bringing back the same veteran-heavy point guard room.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.title: 17-year-old shot in Jackson Park
entries.summary: <p>A teen was shot in Jackson Park Wednesday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The boy, 17, was in a verbal altercation with another person in the park in the 1900 block of East Hayes Drive at 6:47 p.m. when the other person shot him, police said.</p><p>He took himself to University of Chicago Medical Center where he was listed in fair condition.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Boy, 14, shot in thigh during Morgan Park argument
entries.summary: <p>A gunman fled after shooting a 14-year-old boy during an argument early Thursday in the Morgan Park neighborhood on the city's Far South Side, police said. </p><p>The teen was in the 11500 block of South Church Street around 1:45 a.m. when an argument erupted between him and a gunman turned physical and the boy was shot in the right thigh, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Comer Children's Hospital in good condition, police said. </p><p>The attacker fled in an unknown direction and was not arrested. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man killed, 2 wounded in Greater Grand Crossing shooting
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for a white SUV involved in a shooting early Thursday that left a 54-year-old man dead and two other people wounded in the Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood. </p><p>Just after 3 a.m., two men and a woman were in a white car going south in the 7100 block of South Champlain Avenue when a white SUV pulled alongside them and someone inside opened fire, Chicago police said. </p><p>A 54-year-old man was shot in the head and back and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he died, police said. His name was not released.</p><p>A 48-year-old woman was shot in the chest and a second man, 45, was shot in the left leg, police said. They were taken to the University of Chicago where they were both in good condition. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Late Husband's Unknown, Oldest Daughter Makes Contact
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been widowed for seven years. My husband served in the Air Force in Saigon during the conflict in Vietnam. We met and married shortly after he returned from his hitch overseas. We had two daughters together.</p><p>Recently, my older daughter was notified through social media that she has a half-sister, "Leiba," from a woman her father knew in Vietnam. They agreed to meet this weekend for lunch at a local restaurant.</p><p>My daughter asked if I would accompany her to this meeting. I told her that while I had no qualms about finding out he had a child with another woman, I didn't see any point in my being there to meet her. There is no connection there for me, and I would feel uncomfortable in the situation. Am I wrong for not going with my daughters to this luncheon? — <i>UNRELATED IN SOUTH CAROLINA</i></p><p><b>DEAR UNRELATED:</b> Although you feel no connection to your late husband's love child, Leiba is related to your daughters. If they choose to develop a relationship with their half-sister, you cannot ignore her existence forever. Your daughters may be asking for your support. If you decide to go, do it for them.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My son and his partner have lived together for more than 10 years. During this time, his partner's parents and sister have visited my state numerous times. They have stayed at my lake house, in my condo and another home I own. Yet, in all this time, I have never met them (and I have tried to).</p><p>Only once did I receive a thank-you note on my mantle at one of my homes. When they come into town, it's almost like they deliberately avoid meeting me. Is this something I should address with my son and his partner? At this point, I feel hurt. — <i>USED IN THE MIDWEST</i></p><p><b>DEAR USED:</b> Should you address this with your son and his partner? Of course you should. In fact, you should have done it the first time you were asked to let these people live in one of your dwellings. Do you really want to continue having strangers vacation in your homes? Because that's what they have chosen to make themselves, it may be time to roll up the welcome mat.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a daughter, "Imogen," who has been married to her narcissistic and controlling wife, "Brianna," for 20 years. Imogen's relationships with me, my husband and her sister have been entirely dictated by Brianna. We're not allowed in their house, her calls are made from the car, I have not been invited to birthday parties for their two boys, and I'm told not to attend my grandson's swimming competitions if Brianna is in the building.</p><p>Two attempts at divorce by Imogen were unsuccessful, the last one having been a month ago. Imogen appears to be willing to accept verbal abuse and non-negotiable demands from her wife, interpreting the control as caring behavior. This cultlike existence has resulted in resentment and disappointment. I'm at a loss as to how to help my daughter extricate herself from a life of dysfunction and dependency. Any advice would be appreciated. — <i>WORRIED MOM</i></p><p><b>DEAR MOM:</b> Your daughter will not leave Brianna until she's ready, but that doesn't mean you should give up. Avoid criticizing Brianna directly but continue to ask Imogen how Brianna's controlling actions make her feel. Getting her to think along those lines may lead her in the right direction. Above all, make sure she knows about the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233, and remind her that controlling behavior is a form of violence.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: When the men who walked on the moon walked through Chicago
entries.summary: <p>In August of 1969, Chicago welcomed Neil Armstrong, Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin Jr. and Michael Collins to the city only a few weeks after their stop on the moon. entries.title: Pullman to see Starbucks, other eateries open in 2027
entries.summary: <p>As Pullman celebrates the opening of a Chipotle on Thursday, local leaders announced plans to bring a Starbucks, Tropical Smoothie Cafe and Chicago’s first Slim & Husky’s, a pizza chain whose investor includes former Bears running back Matt Forte.</p><p>The three eateries are expected to open late next year at the new Pullman Park Retail Center on 111th Street, Daniel Doig, president of community development group Chicago Neighborhood Initiatives, said.</p><p>“We’re on a roll with these retailers,” Doig said.</p><p>The new center “is a powerful vote of confidence in Pullman's future. Every new investment creates jobs, expands amenities for residents and builds on nearly $1 billion in public and private investment that is reshaping Chicago's Far South Side,” Ald. Anthony Beale (9th) said in a news release.</p><p>The announcement came as Chipotle launched a 1,500-square-foot space with a drive-thru at 11211 S. Corliss Ave. The 8-acre complex, called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/05/09/pullman-gateway-chicago-neighborhood-initiatives-development-breaks-ground" >Pullman Gateway</a>, broke ground in 2024 and is home to Chick-fil-A, Dunkin', Jimmy John's and the Chicago Transit Authority's Red Line Extension project offices.</p><p>“We started on this two years ago. It’s all built-out now. It speaks to the momentum we have,” Doig said. “I’m surprised how quickly it’s filled up. That’s a good thing.”</p><p>About 300 CTA employees work at the site and bring lunchtime traffic, he said. In total, Pullman Gateway’s businesses have created nearly 500 jobs.</p><p>Workers from nearby Amazon, Method and SC Johnson facilities also create demand for restaurants, Doig said. People also come from the nearby Harborside International Golf Course, concerts at the House of Hope arena and Pullman’s tourist sites such as the Pullman National Historical Park.</p><p>Pullman was created in the 1880s as a company town to house workers who made luxury railroad cars at the factory of magnate George Pullman. Yet over the years, industrial decline gutted one of the country’s first planned model industrial towns.</p><p>But since 2009, Pullman and neighboring Roseland have attracted about $900 million in public and private investment and created almost 2,000 permanent jobs, according to a news release from Chicago Neighborhood Initiatives. The nonprofit led Pullman Gateway’s development with the Hope Center Foundation.</p><p>The site of Pullman Gateway was formerly a Hawthorne Racecourse off-track betting facility and parking lot.</p><p>Since 2014, Pullman has seen an influx of corporate investment spurred by local leaders and initiatives. The neighborhood has seen major openings, including a Walmart; the first Whole Foods distribution center in Illinois; the first <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/09/25/gotham-greens-expands-footprint-again-pullman-adds-spinach-new-greenhouse" >Gotham Greens</a> greenhouse outside of New York; and a Method soap plant that was the first factory to open on the South Side in 30 years.</p><p>Until recently, there were only a few restaurants in Pullman. Lexington Betty Smokehouse, Potbelly’s and Culver’s have opened about half a mile from the main Pullman National Park building.</p><p>Otherwise, there were few places where visitors could linger. The nonprofit Pullman House Project expanded the neighborhood’s first cafe in 2024. It's housed in the project’s restored Queen Anne home and visitors’ center at 605 E. 111th St.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/05/09/pullman-gateway-chicago-neighborhood-initiatives-development-breaks-ground" >Pullman Gateway, a new mixed-use development, breaks ground</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: After six months in ICE detention, a Chicago tamale vendor rebuilds her life
entries.summary: <p>Through the window of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicle as it pulled away last September, Laura Murillo could see her tamale stand near the busy Home Depot on 47th Street and Western Avenue. A folding table held coolers, containers and supplies beneath a striped umbrella next to her silver minivan. Only minutes earlier, Murillo, an immigrant from Mexico, had been waiting for her customers.</p><p>The night before her arrest, Murillo had made the tamales in the kitchen of a brick building she rented on the Southeast Side. Before sunrise, she and a worker packed them into her van and she drove to set up her stand.</p><p>For years, Murillo arranged much of her life around this routine. The tamale business allowed the mother of two to care for herself, support her daughters and offer work to other women. While it was grueling work, it was central to how Murillo understood herself: as an independent provider, a business owner and someone others could depend on.</p><p>“Everything was work,” Murillo says now in Spanish, speaking with the confidence of someone accustomed to running things on her own. “It was happiness.”</p><p>But the 55-year-old is now questioning the life she had built around constant work. She <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/27/tamale-vendor-arrested-back-of-the-yards-ice-immigration" target="_blank" ><u>was arrested</u></a> during last fall’s aggressive Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign and spent six months in federal immigration detention.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Murillo returned to Chicago in March, among the small number of immigrants who have been released as a result of a court order rather than deported. She says she’s in the process of obtaining legal status.</p><p>In the meantime, Murillo is making more room for her daughters and accepting their growing independence. And she’s trying to rebuild a new identity around a newfound appreciation for her city, a slower pace of life, her faith and the people she loves.</p><p>“My life is different now. I take it day by day,” Murillo says.</p><h3>The work of caring</h3><p>Murillo first arrived in Chicago in 2005 from Tamaulipas, Mexico, with her then-partner, expecting to stay only a few years. Instead, they found work, raised their daughters, Génesis, now 20, and Daniela, 17, and built a life in the city.</p><p>The young mother first worked in factories before learning the tamale business.</p><p>In 2013, her close friend Gina Otamendi had separated from her husband and was raising four young children when she came to Murillo looking for work.</p><p>Murillo hired her, taught her to make and sell tamales and arranged her hours around her children’s school schedules — giving Otamendi the flexibility she needed as a single mother.</p><p>“She let me leave to feed my children and take them to school because I had to work to pay for everything they needed,” Otamendi says in Spanish. “She gave me food. She always helped me.”</p><p>Otamendi, 50, remembers long hours of making tamales, but also music and laughter. The women competed to see who could make the most tamales in an hour. They sang and danced while they worked.</p><p>“[It was] a very beautiful friendship,” Otamendi says.</p><p>Years later, Otamendi would help Murillo’s daughters while their mother was in detention.</p><p>Otamendi checked on Génesis and Daniela, brought groceries and arranged meals.</p><p>She also connected the family with Centro de Trabajadores Unidos, an immigrant workers’ rights organization where they found an attorney who took Murillo’s case.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Génesis took on more work to pay the bills while attending college. She also became the main point of contact with the attorney handling her mom’s case.</p><p>“Currently, I am a full-time college student doing my best to keep everything together, but my salary cannot cover all the sudden legal and household expenses we are facing,” Génesis wrote on a GoFundMe page in September 2025.</p><p>“I would talk with her,” Otamendi says. “And the poor girl would become desperate and say, ‘Gina, how am I going to do this?’”</p><p>Daniela, whom Murillo describes as having special needs, learned to wash dishes, take out the trash and handle more of her own personal care.</p><p>The community stepped in, too. The morning after Murillo was detained, neighbors and organizers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/27/tamale-vendor-arrested-back-of-the-yards-ice-immigration" target="_blank" ><u>took over her usual spot</u></a>, selling more than 300 of her tamales in about an hour to raise money for her family.</p><h3>Inside detention</h3><p>Murillo was nearly 1,500 miles away at Camp East Montana in El Paso, Tx.</p><p>She met women in detention whose lives outside were beginning to fall away.</p><p>There were older women whose husbands had stopped answering their calls. Some said their children no longer sent money. There were mothers separated from their families, a woman who walked with a cane and another who used a wheelchair.</p><p>One woman, Murillo recalled, had been arrested while watering the yard outside her home.</p><p>“What crimes did they supposedly commit?” Murillo still asks. “They were at their homes.”</p><p>Immigration officers twice asked Murillo to sign voluntary departure papers, but she refused and waited while her attorneys challenged her detention.</p><p>Other women eventually signed, she says, because they had become desperate and no longer believed anyone was coming for them.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b10000" name="image-b10000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Murillo was held at the Camp East Montana immigrant detention center, housed at a U.S. Army base on the outskirts of El Paso, Texas. The facility includes a series of hardened tents in the desert.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Morgan Lee/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Murillo lost 36 pounds during her six months there. She says her faith helped her endure the uncertainty and what she describes as psychological abuse from the guards. A woman from a nearby Catholic shelter visited and read passages from the bible.</p><p>Guards, meanwhile, often reminded the women how little control they had, she says.</p><p>When Murillo asked what time it was, she says they questioned why she needed to know. When she wanted clean socks, she says one told her, “What for? You’re not getting out.”</p><p>Unable to fill the role she had long held at home, Murillo could only speak to her daughters over the phone.</p><p>“What I missed most were my daughters’ little faces,” Murillo says.</p><p>“When they lock you up, you lose control. [My daughters] weren’t calling me anymore to ask me things or ask permission. My daughters were doing things on their own.”</p><p>By last spring, she didn’t have much hope that she would be released. But in late March, the federal government unexpectedly released Murillo after acknowledging that her arrest had violated the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/27/judge-orders-32-detainees-released-over-ice-consent-decree-violations-unclear-how-many-still-in-custody" target="_blank" ><u>Castañón Nava consent decree</u></a>, a 2022 federal court settlement that limited immigration arrests without warrants.</p><p>Upon her release, officers took Murillo to a Catholic shelter in El Paso, where she spent the weekend. Murillo said it took time to understand that she was free. She initially remained inside the shelter until a woman there reminded her that she was allowed to leave. Murillo went for a walk and attended Mass the following morning.</p><p>Her daughters had planned to visit her in detention, and they decided to make the trip anyway to bring their mother home. They arrived that Sunday and flew back with her to Chicago.</p><p>“You know how, in movies, people come out of some ordeal, arrive home and kiss the ground? I almost wanted to do that,” Murillo says. “I swear to you, I truly experienced it that way.”</p><h3>A different life in Chicago</h3><p>Back home, Murillo does not want to rebuild the same life, but she knows she still needs — and wants — to work.</p><p>She has considered opening a small tamalería without the demanding schedule she once kept. Murillo holds out her hands, showing the rheumatoid arthritis she says she has from repeatedly moving between heat and cold while cooking and selling tamales through Chicago winters.</p><p>“I no longer see life as killing myself trying to achieve things,” Murillo says. “Not anymore.”</p><p>Murillo's reluctance to return to her old pace and routine mirrors a similar withdrawal by other street vendors.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d20000" name="image-d20000"></a> <picture </div><p>Nearly a year after Operation Midway Blitz began, leaders of the Street Vendors Association of Chicago said fear continues to determine when — and if — vendors go out to sell.</p><p>Vendors who continue working still risk immigration enforcement, even as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2026/07/10/ice-arrests-increase-chicago-tactics-less-publicized-midway-blitz-back-yards-gage-brighton-park" target="_blank" ><u>ICE agents have carried out arrests more quietly</u></a> than during the height of President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign. Association leaders also said local police officers have increasingly scrutinized street vendors for selling without licenses or in prohibited areas.</p><p>Murillo says she’s in the process of obtaining legal status. She was not comfortable sharing specifics because of her recent detention. Her partner helps with the rent. Génesis started paying for her own phone and internet.</p><p>Murillo is proud of her daughters, though she says it was difficult accepting they had learned to manage much more on their own.</p><p>“I struggle with it a little bit,” Murillo says. “It’s like they don’t need me anymore.”</p><p>Murillo is spending more time with them, including trips to the park and the movies. For years, work came first. “Wait until tomorrow, wait until tomorrow,” she recalls telling them when they wanted to hang out.</p><p>After long defining independence as being able to care for herself and others without asking anyone for help, Murillo now understands how many people had stepped in while she was gone — bringing food, offering money, advice and helping her daughters navigate the months without her.</p><p>“Mami, you have no idea how much people love you,” Murillo recalls Génesis telling her. “You can’t even imagine.”</p><bsp-list-loadmore data-module class="PageListD" entries.title: Free summer YMCA memberships draw 3,000 Chicago teens
entries.summary: <p>Hailey Weathers likes to spend her summers playing volleyball in the sand with her friends at Chicago’s beaches, taking breaks in between games with dips in Lake Michigan.</p><p>But sometimes the 14-year-old feels like adults are scrutinizing everything she and her friends do, especially if they are in a big group. Hailey knows that’s because some large gatherings of teens have become disruptive.</p><p>But being watched and unfairly judged like that makes her feel uncomfortable, she said.</p><p>“Why do teens get blamed for stuff that we’re not doing?” Hailey said.</p><p>That’s why this summer Hailey is also at the South Side YMCA three days a week. She’s in the gym, in the computer lab or chatting with friends.</p><p>Hailey is one of thousands of teens who signed up to be a member this summer through the YMCA of Metropolitan Chicago’s Get Summer program, a partnership with the city offering free memberships to 12- to 18-year-olds. It's Hailey’s first time being a member.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fb0000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Hailey Weathers, who is starting ninth grade at Gary Comer College Prep, said her grandma signed her up for a free summer membership at the South Side YMCA to encourage her to “get out of the house.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Nearly 3,100 teens have registered through the program since June at seven Ys across the city, with the South Side location receiving more than a third of signups. The YMCA couldn’t say how many teens were first-time members, but leaders at participating sites have noticed an uptick in foot traffic and many new faces.</p><p>Some locations with large amounts of newcomers have had space issues, but officials say that’s a good problem to have. Discussions are ongoing about repeating the program next year.</p><p>Hailey, who is going into ninth grade at Gary Comer College Prep, would love to come back.</p><p>“They should do this next summer because it gets me out of the house and I can hang around people I trust,” she said.</p><p>Officials with the YMCA hoped that as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/03/ymca-free-summer-memberships-chicago-teens-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" ><u>many as 5,000 young people</u></a> would sign up by the time the program ends Aug. 31. As of Monday, the organization had logged 3,083 Get Summer registrations.</p><p>Though the organization will likely fall short of its original target, “seeing as though this is our first time launching a program like this, we consider it extremely successful,” a spokesperson for the YMCA said in an email.</p><p>At the South Side Y, 1,179 young people have signed up — the most out of the seven locations offering free memberships. The McCormick YMCA in the Logan Square and Humboldt Park area recorded 510 registrations, the second-most.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d20000" name="html-embed-module-d20000"></a><div style="min-height:923px" id="datawrapper-vis-NSmUq"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/NSmUq/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-NSmUq"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/NSmUq/full.png" alt="Thousands of teens signed up for free YMCA memberships this summer (Symbol map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Officials announced the free membership program after a Memorial Day weekend marred by so-called “teen takeovers,” large gatherings of young people organized on social media that have sometimes turned violent.</p><p>To curb the gatherings, some local officials have suggested stricter curfew laws, more arrests and fines for parents whose children are disruptive. Mayor Brandon Johnson and YMCA officials countered that the better answer is to offer young people more free or affordable activities and safe places to meet.</p><p>The free membership initiative was funded entirely through philanthropic sources, according to a spokesperson for the mayor’s office. Mielle Cares, a foundation that advocates for the mental well-being of young people, created a $250,000 fund to expand youth-centered gathering opportunities in the city, including the Get Summer program.</p><p>Royce Holmes, 15, doesn’t know what the right approach is to keep large teen gatherings safe, but he doesn’t think the solution is to heavily restrict where teens can go. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wsj.com/business/retail/teens-helped-bring-malls-back-to-life-now-theyre-getting-banned-37bdc2a9" target="_blank" ><u>Increasingly, malls, movie theaters</u></a> and other businesses limit when teens can visit without an adult chaperone.</p><p>“I feel like it kind of takes a big chunk of our free will,” Royce said. “For us to be banned from a spot or have to be gone from there at a certain time just doesn’t sound right.”</p><p>Royce, a rising sophomore at Leo Catholic High School, signed up for a free membership at the South Side YMCA this summer, too, though he also worked at the location for a few weeks last year through a summer program.</p><p>He can often be found on the basketball court, fighting for rebounds, dishing out assists and practicing his shooting stroke. He’s noticed more people his age at the location this summer. The increase in members have made pickup games more competitive and fun, he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a the people, especially if I have friends with me, but I just don’t want to stay around those types of things for too long because they just become takeovers,” he said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kevin McGowan, who was senior executive director of the South Side YMCA until earlier this month, said the basketball gym is one of the most popular gathering spaces for the new teen members. The location’s pool, fitness center and computer lab are also crowded.</p><p>McGowan said sign-ups at the South Side location have exceeded expectations, but they haven’t maxed out their capacity. To manage the flow, staff keep tabs on activity schedules and let teens know when spaces are available to them. Plus, teens don’t show up all at once, they trickle in throughout the day.</p><p>“It's crowded in here, no doubt, but we haven't really had an issue with too many people in the building,” McGowan said. “Of course, the old people don't like having young people around, but they get over it.”</p><p>He thinks the South Side location has seen the most new teen registrations because there aren’t many places in the area where kids have lots of options to keep busy and just be themselves.</p><p>On the Northwest Side, the pool at the McCormick YMCA has been one of the most active spots for young people this summer, according to Mallory Munzel, who oversees youth programming at YMCAs across the city.</p><p>The new crowds there have led staff to be judicious about how many people are allowed in the gym at the same time, but they haven’t had any other issues with capacity, Munzel said.</p><p>“It’s exciting to see this many teens in the building every day,” she added. “I would imagine based on the level of engagement that, probably, we will do it again.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>So far, more than 3,000 teens have taken advantage of a new program offering free memberships at seven YMCA locations this summer. The South Side Y had the most sign-ups.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>While many teens come in to play basketball, swim or lift weights, some don’t feel like doing anything in particular, Munzel said.</p><p>Youth-centered programs often forget: Sometimes all a teen needs is a space that allows them to do nothing, and there aren’t many places for teens to do that, she said. Chicago Ys have couches where teens can relax and vending machines with snacks in the common areas. The South Side Y has a “teen lounge” with video games and a ping pong table.</p><p>“Some of them just want to hang out with their friends,” Munzel said “They’re just here to chill.”</p><p>Royce and Hailey prefer being in smaller groups. They have come across flyers on social media for large gatherings at the beach or Downtown but they avoid them because they’ve also seen videos of the disruptions that can break out.</p><p>They both plan on telling friends and young family members about the YMCA’s programs so they know about those alternatives.</p><p>“It’s easier to have a good time here,” Royce said, “It feels more free.”</p>

entries.summary: <p>Like that kid at your high school who was somehow always a step ahead of everyone else in listening to the next cool band, Chicago theater audiences recently have been given plenty of opportunities to crow about seeing future hits before the rest of the country.</p><p>“The Notebook,” for example, is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2026/08/07/review-touring-production-of-the-notebook-nederlander-theatre-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>playing now</u></a> at the Nederlander Theatre on tour class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“Illinoise” had a major-theater debut also at Chicago Shakespeare, in 2024, from which it went off-Broadway, then to Broadway.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Liz Lauren</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The first thing to recognize about the life cycle of a show is that the show is alive. That is to say, it’s always evolving, and not only in its so-called out-of-town tryout phase. (That is to say, the town it’s “out of” is New York.)</p><p>“That's what I love about musicals,” said producer Kevin McCollum, whose resume lists lines for “Rent,” “Avenue Q” and “In the Heights,” all of which won him Tonys. “They're living organisms.”</p><p>For “The Notebook,” McCollum came to Chicago Shakespeare to propose an out-of-town tryout. McCollum had a pre-existing connection with the theater, on projects such as the North American premiere of “Six” and the American premiere of “Ride the Cyclone,” and dating back to the germ of his time attending high school in Deerfield.</p><p>From a producer’s perspective, a theater like Chicago Shakes has a built-in audience. And in Chicago, it’s a high-quality audience, McCollum said.</p><p>“They’re sophisticated, they’re smart, they’re generous, but they also tell you where you are,” he said. They won’t mince words on misfires. “Chicago audiences are very honest. You know where you stand.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2f0000" name="image-2f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e0a46fa/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F06%2F43%2Fb3de6b3f41ac93f92289f6d6907c%2Fgettyimages-2278353903.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/08d0024/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F06%2F43%2Fb3de6b3f41ac93f92289f6d6907c%2Fgettyimages-2278353903.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0b549a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F06%2F43%2Fb3de6b3f41ac93f92289f6d6907c%2Fgettyimages-2278353903.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Kevin McCollum attends the 2026 New Dramatists Spring Luncheon at The New York Marriott Marquis on May 26, 2026 in New York City. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0b549a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F06%2F43%2Fb3de6b3f41ac93f92289f6d6907c%2Fgettyimages-2278353903.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/92dcc34/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F06%2F43%2Fb3de6b3f41ac93f92289f6d6907c%2Fgettyimages-2278353903.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0b549a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F06%2F43%2Fb3de6b3f41ac93f92289f6d6907c%2Fgettyimages-2278353903.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“Chicago audiences are very honest. You know where you stand,” producer Kevin McCollum said. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>It makes sense for theaters to take the gamble. The theater gets a buzzy new work, lots of good publicity if they partner with shows that succeed, and in many cases, a small percentage of revenues for the ongoing life of the show.</p><p>Kimberly Motes, the executive director of Chicago Shakespeare Theater, acknowledged the hot streak lately for her theater with shows transferring to Broadway and elsewhere. In addition to “The Notebook” and “Illinoise,” in the past few years Chicago Shakes also transferred <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2025/10/09/paranormal-activity-chicago-shakespeare-levi-holloway" target="_blank" ><u>“Paranormal Activity,” </u></a><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2024/07/12/lord-of-the-rings-musical-chicago-shakespeare-theater" target="_blank" ><u>“The Lord of the Rings”</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2025/03/31/the-kinks-sunny-afternoon-revew-chicago-shakespeare-theater" target="_blank" ><u>“Sunny Afternoon”</u></a> — all of which germinated in England before heading to Chicago — to prominent stages in other cities.</p><p>These shows are partnerships between the outside producers and the theaters, sometimes from as early in the process as acquiring rights to use source material. Theaters can help with casting, design, publicity and anything else where they have networks and experience in place. The commercial producers bring their own networks and investors. “The commercial producer may provide the resources for things that are beyond what we would normally do if we were producing it ourselves,” Motes said.</p><p>Motes said it’s not just the sophistication that enamors Chicago to producers, but also the openness. “In other markets it might be arms folded, leaning back, saying, ‘Show me.’ Chicago audiences lean forward, open their arms and say, ‘Show me!’” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure but also the openness.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Chicago Shakespeare Theater</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>And clearly, it’s cheaper. McCollum said the jump from Chicago to Broadway took “The Notebook” from a $3 million endeavor to a $15 million endeavor. Once on Broadway, there’s a black-and-white definition of success: “A hit is a show that returns the money,” McCollum said, meaning the show earns back in revenue what was initially invested.</p><p>A longtime adage states that one out of five Broadway shows recoup their initial investment. But perhaps the more critical problem now is the reluctance to open them: Last season, the New York Times noted <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/24/theater/broadway-new-musical-theater.html" target="_blank" ><u>only six new musicals</u></a> opening on Broadway, compared to 15 the year prior, and detailed how the rising costs of staging them <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/22/theater/broadway-musicals-finances.html" target="_blank" ><u>far exceeds ticket prices.</u></a> Plays appeared to fare better.</p><p>But looking only at recouping investment is shortsighted, McCollum said. Even setting aside the question of artistic versus commercial success, shows can have long and complicated lives. They exist in counterpoint with the zeitgeist, McCollum said, and you never know when they might get renewed recognition.</p><p>Stephen Sondheim’s “Merrily We Roll Along,” for instance, flopped in its 1981 debut, but has had a significant afterlife, including a successful revival in 2023. As another example, the production of “Chicago” that has run for nearly 30 years on Broadway is a revival.</p><p>The Broadway run is meaningful for advertising to audiences — you can say a show is a Broadway show once it’s had one — but it isn’t the be-all and end-all. “Broadway is an important part of the life of the show,” McCollum said. “I think you have to look at it as the launch McCollum said “The Notebook” did not recoup on Broadway, even though it had a solid nine-month run. But so far the tour has done well.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Roger Mastroianni</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A possible next phase after a Broadway run begins — but not necessarily after it ends — is touring. Some shows excel in New York and fizzle on tour; others the opposite. McCollum said “The Notebook” did not recoup on Broadway, even though it had a solid nine-month run. But so far the tour has done well, and in yet another evolutionary phase, the producers are licensing productions in other countries, such as the Philippines, Brazil and Germany.</p><p>Although it seems counterintuitive, it can be good for a tour when a show closes on Broadway, because the assets of the New York production can be repurposed. Sets, costumes and sometimes performers can go on the buses and trucks and save the producers having to re-create or recast.</p><p>Which brings us back to “Illinoise.” Shows don’t have to tour to live on beyond their New York run; sometimes they just need a theater to champion a remount. Motes and Chicago Shakes wanted “Illinoise” back.</p><p>“It did not have the national tour,” Motes said. “As we were planning the 40th anniversary season, Edward Hall, our artistic director, and I felt like this was unfinished business.”</p><p>Unfinished business is one way to put it. Another might be rebirth.</p>

entries.title: PHOTOS: Loop's iconic weather bell back in action
entries.summary: <p>Look up: The long-dormant Bell Federal Savings weather sign outside the Rector Building, 79 W. Monroe St., is now back in action. </p><p>The 1950s sign that features a lighted, acrylic bell that changes color according to anticipated weather conditions has been restored. entries.title: Maybe adults should follow students in setting down our phones
entries.summary: <p>My high school had a smoking lounge. But don't let the term "lounge" fool you. There were no comfy chairs, no billiard table, not even any walls. It was outside, behind the school, a weedy area where students would gather before, after, and, I imagine, during class to get their nicotine fix.</p><p>This was in the late '70s. And if today it seems wildly inappropriate that a public school would facilitate smoking among teenagers, remember, back then smoking was considered nearly a human right, and there was a problem they were trying to address: smoke-filled restrooms. At least the lounge got smokers outside where they wouldn't impose their vice upon others.</p><p>Memories of the smoking lounge wafted into mind while I was on medical leave, when Illinois joined 38 states allowing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/07/28/illinois-school-cellphone-ban-signed-law-jb-pritzker" >cell phones to be banned</a> during school next year.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a80000" name="module-a80000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>When Illinois first contemplated the ban, I was against it. Phones are part of our lives now, like auxiliary limbs. Schools would do better teaching kids restraint regarding their phones since they will be constant companions after graduation. The focus should be on harm reduction.</p><p>Then I thought about the situation some more and, through a superpower of mine called "changing my mind," decided that the ban is right. It helps that social media has degraded into an odious AI slop sink. Facebook imagines that my being Jewish means I want to view an endless loop of every antisemitic incident anywhere on earth, interspersed with agitprop about Israel, plus trite little tales about the Holocaust, which is being retrofitted into a feel good story of heroism, resistance, and survival.</p><p>Spoiler alert: it wasn't.</p><p>Meanwhile, Instagram served up so many snippets of "The West Wing" that I finally realized I could just watch "The West Wing" on Netflix and cut out the middleman. That's when I thought of smoking in school. We are biased toward the present and it's hard to imagine things changing. But change they do and today's necessity becomes tomorrow's puzzling affliction. Someday people gaping at their phones could be viewed with the same disapproval extended toward the miserable knot of coworkers puffing around the office entrance.</p><p>Social media is so harmful to teens, so toxic, schools are right to teach youth there is life outside their screens. And the smoking lounge made me wonder whether high schools might not only be right regarding phones, but a vanguard, pointing society toward where we should all be going, as they were with cigarettes.</p><p>In 1978, when I graduated from high school, the smoking rate among American adults was 36%. Today it is 10%, a triumph over damaging addiction, with countless years of life saved. (Though that might change now that the federal government is getting out of the "help people stay healthy" business).</p><p>Illinois banned smoking in high schools in 1990. Eighteen years passed before the state got around to banning smoking in restaurants. At the time, it was unimaginable — to not light up after a meal! Calamity. The restaurant industry would <i>die</i>. We journalists were dead set against it — what would a newsroom be if you couldn't grind out your cigarette on the tile floor? (The Sun-Times had its own smoking lounge; a truly repulsive little room that did have chairs, plus an enormous air purifier. I would go there sometimes to smoke a cigar and listen to Art Petacque reminisce about the mob).</p><p>While it's premature to predict society turning up its nose at phones, hints are there. Flip-phones are back. My two boys look at social media with a mix of contempt and indifference: it's something old people do to spritz the illusion of significance over their empty lives. I didn't even post the birth of my most recent grandchild — No. 3! — on Facebook, since his parents' attitude about the platform — a grotesque nest of senior citizens posting photos of lunch that nobody wants to see — had infected me. Plus I didn't want to get in trouble.</p><p>Now that my boys are adults, I try not to write about them much. They live their own private lives. But I do remember visiting my younger son in law school and watching him drop his phone into a hard plastic lockbox with a timer, so he could have no access to the phone for a certain span of hours while he studied. Back then it seemed almost an admission of lack of control. Just ignore it. But now I see how smart that was. </p><p>Big Tech is making a huge gamble, investing hundreds of billions of dollars in the certainty we're going to surrender to AI and let it do all our thinking for us. Maybe we will. But maybe we won't. And maybe our schools can lead the way.</p>

entries.title: Woman, 58, fatally struck by roofing material during Gary, Ind. storm
entries.summary: <p>A woman was fatally struck by roofing material during damaging storms Tuesday afternoon in Gary, Indiana. </p><p>Paula Plebanski, 58, was found by the Lake County Coroner's Office around 12:20 p.m. Tuesday in a parking lot in the 5200 block of East Dunes Highway, the coroner's office said. </p><p>Her death was caused by multiple blunt force injuries and was ruled an accident, officials said. </p><p>In Portage, Indiana, 86-year-old Leona Rice was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/12/portage-home-explosion-storm-damage-cleanup" target="_blank" >killed in a home explosion</a> just as severe storms were beginning to sweep through the area Tuesday. It remains unclear if storms directly contributed to the explosion. </p>

target="_blank" >After 6 months in ICE detention, a tamale vendor rebuilds her life</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydlyqlt-l-o/" target="_blank" >Alma Campos</a></h5><p><b>Chicagoan detained</b>: Through the window of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicle last September, Laura Murillo could see her tamale stand near 47th Street and Western Avenue. Murillo, 55, immigrated from Mexico in 2005 then spent nearly 15 years in the tamale business, work that allowed her to support her two daughters. Then she was arrested and spent six months in federal immigration detention.</p><p><b>Inside detention</b>: Murillo was taken nearly 1,500 miles away to a facility in El Paso, Texas. She said she experienced psychological abuse from the guards and met women whose lives outside were beginning to fall away. She had started to lose hope until March, when the federal government unexpectedly released her after acknowledging her arrest had violated a consent decree that limited immigration arrests without warrants.</p><p><b>Different life</b>: Murillo's daughters, 20 and 17, brought her back to Chicago, where Murillo has been trying to rebuild a different life. She said she's in the process of obtaining legal status and wants to find work outside of the grueling vendor business. She has also been trying to spend more time with her daughters, who told her how many people stepped in to help while she was detained, offering food, money and overall support. "Mami, you have no idea how much people love you. ... You can’t even imagine," her daughter told her. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydlyqlt-l-b/" target="_blank" >String lights not permitted under little-known municipal code rule</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydlyqlt-l-a/" target="_blank" >Stephanie Zimmermann</a></h5><p><b>Lights out</b>: String lights, those decorative flourishes adorning hundreds of outdoor dining areas in the city, aren’t allowed in the public way. That's according to an inspector from the Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection, who recently had Mitch Einhorn, co-owner of Lush Wine & Spirits in Roscoe Village, take his lights down.</p><p><b>Code word</b>: In an email, a BACP spokesperson said that "under the Municipal Code of Chicago, string lights are not permitted in sidewalk cafes." It's unclear why they aren't allowed. BACP just said it "conducts complaint-driven investigations at businesses throughout the City of Chicago to ensure compliance with Chicago's Municipal Code," and those usually originate with calls to 311.</p><p><b>What to do?</b> Einhorn said he doesn't know who filed the complaint about his lights, and he's ticked off that the inspector didn't walk Roscoe Street to see the other businesses with similar white lights. He asked BACP if he could apply for a special use permit for the lights but was told no such permit exists.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydlyqlt-l-f/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>LET’S HEAR FROM YOU 🗣️</h4><p>Have you switched to a concierge doctor or to a doctor at a direct primary care practice? James</a></h5><p>Local researchers and bird-lovers were in awe this spring when they spotted a rare bird with both male and female characteristics at a nature preserve in suburban Barrington.</p><p>The mysterious bird, a bobolink, was identified as a bilateral gynandromorph: The bird’s body was divided down the middle, with one side having male characteristics and the other side female.</p><p>Luke Dahlberg, a conservation seed program manager with Citizens for Conservation and longtime birder, first encountered the bird May 10 at the organization's Hill 'N Dale Preserve. entries.title: 5 tornadoes confirmed from Tuesday's storms, bringing state total up to 205 for the year
entries.summary: <p>Five tornadoes have been confirmed related to Tuesday's severe weather, bringing Illinois' total up to 205 twisters for the year. </p><p>The tornadoes touched down in Oswego, Wilmington, Mokena to Tinley Park, Orland Park to Munster, Indiana and Monee to St. John, Indiana, the National Weather Service confirmed. </p><p>The worst of the tornadoes hit Monee and St. John, with wind speeds peaking around 115 mph, according to the weather service. </p><p>That twister was an EF-2 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, which rates the strength and related damage for tornadoes. Of the remaining 4, 3 were classified as EF-1 and one was EF-0, officials said. EF-5 is the highest rating.</p><p>More than eight months into the year, Illinois has already broken the record for most tornadoes recorded in a single year, shattering the previous record of 142 in 2024. </p><p>The total may climb with more severe weather forecasted for central Illinois. A severe thunderstorm watch with conditions that may spawn a couple of tornadoes was in effect for Kankakee, Blommington and Champaign among other areas, according to the weather service. </p>
