entries.title: 44 candidates likely to appear on Chicago school board ballot
entries.summary: <p>The city’s Board of Elections settled the last handful of objections to school board candidates this week, paving the way for 44 of the initial 51 people who threw their hat in the race to appear on the ballot in November.</p><p>The elections board overruled objections to the candidacies of sitting school board members Michilla Blaise, who represents a West Side district, and Karen Zaccor, whose district is on the North Side. Hopefuls Claudia Peralta and Connie Anderson also survived challenges.</p><p>However the board sustained objections against Kernetha Jones because she didn’t specify which district she planned to run in and removed her from the ballot.</p><p>With Tuesday’s decisions, the slate of candidates in this fall’s elections, when Chicago residents will elect all 21 school board members for the first time, is nearly finalized. Six candidates who were previously cleared by the city elections board are facing appeals in Cook County Circuit Court.</p><p>Unless any of those decisions are overturned, there will be 44 school board candidates, five of whom are running for board president.</p><p>In all, seven candidates were kicked off the ballot due to objections. That includes Angel Velez, who represents a Southwest Side district and is the board vice president, and Cydney Wallace, who represents a South Side district.</p><p>Five of the 20 district races are now uncontested, leaving residents in parts of the North, Southwest and South sides with little say over who represents them on the school board.</p><p>More candidates were removed from the ballot in 2024, when school board elections were held for the first time. That year, 16 of the 47 people who initially filed to run were kicked off the ballot, leaving 31 candidates. But only half of the school board seats were up for grabs.</p><p>Some board hopefuls taken off the ballot this year expressed frustration at having to defend themselves against objections in what they said was a time-consuming and costly process.</p><p>Objectors often challenge whether candidates have enough valid signatures on their nominating paperwork. Common objections allege that petitions contain duplicate names, wrong or incomplete addresses and other issues.</p><p>Each case is treated like a mini-trial with both sides presenting evidence before the elections board makes a final decision. Candidates often hire lawyers. But not all can afford legal representation, leading some to question whether the objections process unfairly limits who can seek office.</p>
entries.author: Emmanuel Camarillo

entries.title: Cleaning staffer dies days after caught in crossfire of Little Village shooting
entries.summary: <p>An autopsy is scheduled Thursday for a cleaning employee on his way home from work who died days after he was shot early Saturday in the Little Village neighborhood. </p><p>Armando Viveros Cortes, 35, was among a group of four employees in a vehicle returning home from work around 2:40 a.m. Saturday in the 2400 block of South Central Park Avenue when gunfire rang out and Viveros Cortes was struck in the head, Chicago police said. </p><p>Viveros Cortes' co-workers, who initially thought the blasts were fireworks, then drove to the Ogden District police station and honked their horn until officers came outside to assist, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times. </p><p>The victim, who was a backseat passenger, was then taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, where he was pronounced dead Wednesday, police said. </p><p>At least 27 shell casings and seven nine-millimeter casings were found at the scene, according to the police report. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Shedd Aquarium to receive four more beluga whales from Marineland
entries.summary: <p><i>Update, 8-13: The second batch of rescued beluga whales arrived at Shedd Aquarium Thursday morning, after being flown in from Toronto overnight, an aquarium spokesman said. All four — females, ranging in age from 20 to 27 — are doing well, said the spokesman, Johnny Ford.</i></p><p>Shedd Aquarium’s beluga whale population is about to double from what it was a month ago.</p><p>Four more of the white cetaceans are expected to leave the shuttered Marineland Canada this week, arriving in Chicago early Thursday if all goes to plan.</p><p>That’s a big “if,” given the storms that continue to sweep through the region.</p><p>On Wednesday morning, Shedd staff were in Niagara Falls, Canada, preparing the steel boxes used to transport the belugas — first by truck, then inside a Boeing 777 cargo plane flying from Toronto to Chicago, with one stop along the way: The same flight will also carry two more Marineland belugas headed to Georgia Aquarium.</p><div The whale is among four belugas from the shuttered Marineland park expected to arrive at the Shedd Aquarium Thursday. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Shedd Aquarium/Brenna Hernandez</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“We are making sure we have everything that we need … from duct tape to making sure we have the appropriate foam and all the appropriate [beluga] stretcher sizes. This operation is so complex and every animal is different, and we tailor all of the transport equipment per animal,” said Charlie Jacobsma, Shedd’s director of animal behavior and training.</p><p>The incoming whales — all females, named Caspian, Peekachu, Rain and Secord — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/21/4-beluga-whales-arrive-at-shedd-aquarium" >will join four other beluga rescues that arrived from Marineland July 21</a>. In total, Shedd is expected to house 16 belugas, including the eight already living at the aquarium before the Marineland whales arrived.</p><p>The Marineland belugas, a group of 30, had been living at the park, which has for years faced criticism that its animals were living in unsanitary conditions. The park closed to the public in 2024 and Marineland officials, citing extreme financial difficulties, had threatened to euthanize the whales if permanent homes couldn’t be found.</p><p>None of the Marineland belugas has yet been put on display to the public at Shedd, and there is no timeline for when that might happen.</p><p>“If you have a rescue dog that is still learning to be confident in their new surroundings, you’re not going to take the dog to a dog park the first day that you have him and introduce him to all these new stimuli,” Jacobsma said.</p><p>The plan is to run some tests on the four incoming whales, and if the animals are found to be healthy, then they’ll be grouped with the four other rescued belugas.</p><p>Shedd uses a series of gates to separate the mammal groups.</p><p>“In some rare instances, some of the belugas at Shedd have shared the same space [with the Marineland whales], but mostly it has been through the gates,” said Shedd spokesman Johnny Ford.</p><p>The current goal is for Shedd to take a total of 10 belugas from Marineland, although an exact timeline for when the remaining two might travel to Chicago has not been determined, Shedd staff said.</p><p>Asked about the cost of the operation to remove all 30 whales — others are traveling to aquariums in Georgia, Texas, California and Spain — Ford said it is “projected to go into the millions,” primarily covered by the receiving aquariums.</p><p>Ford said the cost would not be passed along to Shedd visitors in the form of increased ticket prices.</p><p>“This is not what we had in our budgets this year, but it was something that we felt called to do as an obligation to these animals. This is something out of our own savings,” Ford said.</p><p>Andrew Burns, a longtime adviser and lawyer for Marineland, said Wednesday that the closed aquatic park has also committed “millions” to the move.</p><p>“All its available funds were committed to this move,” Burns said. “So we’ve made a massive financial commitment ourselves.”</p><p>With the expected departure of six belugas this week, Marineland will be left with 11 whales.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/22/belugas-chicago-shedd-aquarium-marineland-canada-rescue" >Rescued belugas have arrived in Chicago. The move is unprecedented — and controversial</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/23/canadian-belugas-rescue-shedd-aquarium-imminent-risk-lawyer-marineland" >Canadian belugas faced ‘imminent risk’ of death before emergency flight to Chicago, marine park lawyer says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-history/2026/08/07/beluga-whale-shedd-aquarium-abbott-oceanarium" >When Shedd Aquarium’s first beluga whales came to Chicago</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears remain committed to Indiana stadium plan — though they won't rule out Illinois
entries.summary: <p>Bears president/CEO Kevin Warren reiterated Thursday that the team is remained focused on building a stadium in Hammond, Ind. — but once again stopped short of fully committing to moving the Bears across state lines.</p><p>The Bears have finished their due diligence at the Lost Marsh site in Hammond and deemed it "viable," Warren said. The team is currently evaluating the nearby Wolf Lake Terminal site. The Bears could decide to merge parts of both sites together. Warren would not give a timeline for when the Bears could make a decision.</p><p>He said the Bears have had "minimal" conversations with Illinois representatives since the team's board of directors said June 5, they announced the team's board of directors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/05/bears-hammond-indiana-board-directors-vote-stadium-arlington-heights-nfl" target="_blank" >voted to “advance our stadium development project in Hammond</a>." About three weeks later, the team confirmed it began environmental testing at Wolf Lake Terminal, which is west of Interstate 90 and near their original proposed plot in Hammond.</p><p>Earlier Thursday, Gov. J.B. Pritzker told reporters that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> have various desires they've communicated to the state but that they've yet to put them in writing. Late last month, he said he presumed the Bears would tell him "in short order" what exactly they need in a stadium funding bill. The Bears have talked at length about needing a property tax break to build on the 326-acre Arlington Heights plot they own in the northwest suburbs.</p><p>Asked about why the Bears have only had minimal discussions with Illinois lawmakers, chairman George McCaskey said that "if there are substantive discussions to be had, let's have 'em."</p><p>Pritzker hasn't ruled out calling a special session sometime before the regular October session to vote on a stadium funding plan.</p><p>As for the team name: they will remain the Chicago Bears, McCaskey said, whether their next stadium is in Hammond or Arlington Heights. </p><p>Thursday marked the first time that Warren and McCaskey had spoken at length since the June announcement, which was merely a press release presented without further comment. McCaskey and Warren typically give a press conference during training camp each year.<br></p>

entries.title: Review: J. Cole’s ‘The Fall-Off World Tour’ is an endearing homage to his long career and his roots
entries.summary: <p>With Chicago being a key city of the “blog era” in hip-hop, J. Cole’s bond with the Windy City was, and remains, strong. The rapper was one of the artists to break out during this transformative period in hip-hop culture. Sixteen years after dropping his first album, “Cole World: The Sideline Story,” he’s become one of the most revered and successful rappers of his generation. “The Fall-Off World Tour” is an endearing homage to both J. Cole’s long career and his devotion to his hometown, through the good and the bad.</p><p>And with the Windy City being a pivotal place throughout his career, he clearly appreciates the city’s legacy.</p><p>“Y’all from such a f------ legendary, historic city,” Cole told the audience about his reverence for Chicago on Tuesday, the first of two shows at the United Center. “Y’all witnessed greatness on such a high level. The rappers y’all gave to the world, the music, the culture, the slang. Y’all got so much s--- that I don’t know if y’all really know ...”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-160000" name="image-160000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/008ea09/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3500x1964+0+271/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2F9c%2F50e57f3e492dbb7704bbbbeeed88%2Fjcole-260813-012.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/541b5a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3500x1964+0+271/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2F9c%2F50e57f3e492dbb7704bbbbeeed88%2Fjcole-260813-012.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/65073dc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3500x1964+0+271/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2F9c%2F50e57f3e492dbb7704bbbbeeed88%2Fjcole-260813-012.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="J. Cole performs Tuesday at United Center, the first of two shows in Chicago as part of “The Fall-Off World Tour.” " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/65073dc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3500x1964+0+271/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2F9c%2F50e57f3e492dbb7704bbbbeeed88%2Fjcole-260813-012.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4d86b38/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3500x1964+0+271/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2F9c%2F50e57f3e492dbb7704bbbbeeed88%2Fjcole-260813-012.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/65073dc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3500x1964+0+271/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2F9c%2F50e57f3e492dbb7704bbbbeeed88%2Fjcole-260813-012.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>J. Cole performs Tuesday at United Center, the first of two shows in Chicago as part of “The Fall-Off World Tour.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Barry Brecheisen/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>After an opening montage of credits, Cole appeared in the upper level among his fans, performing the six-minute “39 Intro” from the second disc of “The Fall-Off.” As soon as the video screens cut to his face underneath the blue lights, he launched into his opening verse in the upper section with his fans who captured every moment on their phones. Watching him rap his way through the crowd and across both sides of the arena floor, shaking hands along the way, felt like watching a true people’s champion at work.</p><p>Throughout Cole’s career, he’s connected with his fans directly and on a human level. <a class="Link" href="https://www.complex.com/music/a/jaelaniturnerwilliams/j-cole-picks-up-fans-trunk-sale-tour-fall-off" target="_blank" ><u>He recently traveled the country in his vintage Honda Civic</u></a> to promote “The Fall-Off,” selling the album for $1 out of his trunk, and had fans ride with him to listen to the double album.</p><p><b></b> Fan engagement is a major part of the show. During his verse on Benny the Butcher’s “Johnny P’s Caddy,” he invited a fan from the crowd to rap the song with him. He found a young woman in the 100 section behind him with a Dreamville Records jersey and a sign that read “Been Ready From The Night I Was Born.” She electrified the crowd, rapping every word as if her life depended on it. <b></b></p><p>His hometown of Fayetteville, North Carolina, which he affectionately calls “The Ville,” was as much of the main character of the show as Cole was. He rapped in front of and atop a recreation of Fayetteville’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.distinctlyfayettevillenc.com/listing/market-house/7361/" target="_blank" ><u>Market House</u></a>, a U.S. National Historic Landmark and town hall, for the entire show. The setting was especially effective during his performance of emotionally striking songs “Run A Train” and his final song “Quik Stop.” </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4a0000" name="image-4a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4116008/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1748x981+0+92/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F63%2Ff9960be14c559ebfdc7dc16f8ee4%2Fjcole-260813-006a.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/622502a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1748x981+0+92/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F63%2Ff9960be14c559ebfdc7dc16f8ee4%2Fjcole-260813-006a.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/27933c1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1748x981+0+92/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F63%2Ff9960be14c559ebfdc7dc16f8ee4%2Fjcole-260813-006a.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="J. Cole performs Tuesday at United Center, the first of two shows in Chicago as part of “The Fall-Off World Tour.” " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/27933c1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1748x981+0+92/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F63%2Ff9960be14c559ebfdc7dc16f8ee4%2Fjcole-260813-006a.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dcb6b86/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1748x981+0+92/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F63%2Ff9960be14c559ebfdc7dc16f8ee4%2Fjcole-260813-006a.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/27933c1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1748x981+0+92/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F00%2F63%2Ff9960be14c559ebfdc7dc16f8ee4%2Fjcole-260813-006a.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>J. Cole performs Tuesday at United Center, the first of two shows in Chicago as part of “The Fall-Off World Tour.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Barry Brecheisen/For the Sun-Tim</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Even the white towels laid on every seat for attendees served a purpose. Fans were ceremoniously twirling them in the air during “Old Dog” in homage to North Carolina sports culture and fellow North Carolina rapper Petey Pablo. The tribute continued when he played Pablo’s 2001 hit, “Raise Up.”</p><p><b></b> “The Fall-Off” tour featured a unique segment called “Dreamville Radio,” hosted by Dreamville veteran Bas and DJ Dummy, to introduce fans to the label’s roster and rising acts. It felt like a live, underground mix show. DJ Dummy energized the crowd with hip-hop and R&B hits from the ‘90s, 2000s, and 2010s. Bas brought out North Carolina artists, singer/songwriter PJ and rapper PFG (Prettyface Gangsta), and Chicago rapper Omen to rock the crowd. Before Bas performed his verses from “Night Job,” “H.Y.B.,” and “Tribe,” he conducted short Q&As with each artist after their set. </p><p>Cole’s performance of fan favorite “Middle Child” was one of the night's most anticipated moments that leaned into his aggressive determination to be one of the best rappers. <b></b></p><p>The Day 1 fans got their money’s worth with Cole’s generous set list that dug deep into his early catalog. The invigorating energy that filled the arena continued during Cole’s “Nobody’s Perfect.” The whole United Center sang the whole song word-for-word without him even rapping a bar.</p><p>It’s that lifelong connection to his fans combined with the conviction in his music that has allowed him to be in the proverbial “Big 3” conversation in mainstream rap. Arguably more than his undeniably skilled lyricism, it’s landmark performances like this that show why Cole, despite the album’s title, will never fall off.</p>

entries.title: What to know after latest round of tornadoes tear through the Chicago suburbs
entries.summary: <p>As hundreds of thousands of Illinois and northwest Indiana residents remain without power following severe storms that brought at least five tornadoes to the area Tuesday, another threat of severe weather — with potentially twister-like winds — was moving through the area Wednesday. </p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/12/more-severe-storms-damaging-winds-may-hit-south-suburbs-over-142-000-still-without-power-in-chicago-area" target="_blank" >severe thunderstorm watch</a> was in effect for Joliet, Kankakee, DeKalb until 1 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. Severe weather could bring downpours and gusty winds, though the storms may not be as strong as Tuesday’s storms.</p><p>“Most areas are not gonna see severe winds, but if you do, you could see winds as high as 70 miles per hour,” Gino Izzi, a meteorologist with the weather service said.</p><p>Residents in Illinois and northwest Indiana were left reeling from Tuesday's storms, where five tornadoes with gusts of 86 to 110 mph were confirmed Tuesday: One in southern Cook County, another in eastern Will County, and the third in the Mokena area, also in Will County.</p><p>In south suburban Mokena, where one of the three confirmed tornadoes hit, winds took down trees and cut power to many homes.</p><p>Rick Johnson, a Mokena resident of more than 30 years, said he’s never experienced so many powerful and destructive storms in a single summer.</p><p>“It’s been an odd year,” he said.</p><p>With more tornado-like conditions approaching the Chicago area and northwest Indiana, here's what you need to know. </p><h3><b>Why are there so many tornadoes in Illinois this year?</b></h3><p>So far this year, Illinois has experienced a record number of tornadoes.</p><p>Meteorologists say multiple rounds of severe weather this spring and summer have contributed to the elevated tornado count.</p><p>Illinois has already shattered the state record for most tornadoes in a year. According to preliminary numbers from the National Weather Service, Illinois has recorded 205 tornadoes as of Aug. 13. The highest mark the state recorded before this year was 142 twisters in 2024.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a state climatologist Trent Ford said every Midwesterner should have the proper plans in place in the event of severe weather warnings in order to make sure family members are safe, together and know what to do. Things like going down into the basement, if you have one, and keeping your phone and other electronic items charged in case of outages. Also make sure to follow messaging from the National Weather Service.</p><p>Some residents admitted they, like Rob Griffin in Lansing, underestimated past storms despite emergency alerts being sent to cellphones and the blaring of tornado sirens.</p><p>“I think they’re doing a good job of warning us,” said Griffin, who lost nearly all of his roof during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/28/storms-flooding-tornadoes-damage-worker-missing-power-outage" >late July’s severe storms</a>. “Hopefully, we, as citizens, will take heed to that.”</p><h3><b>Are tornadoes becoming more common in Illinois?</b></h3><p>While tornado activity can change from year to year, 2026’s activity has reached the highest point in recent years.</p><p>Still, it doesn’t mean Illinois is the new Tornado Alley. Yet.</p><p>According to some definitions, Illinois actually has been considered part of Tornado Alley for some time. Initially, the nickname applied to Southwestern states ravaged by twisters in the last century, such as Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.</p><h3><b>Is climate change causing more tornadoes?</b></h3><p>The answer isn’t straightforward.</p><p>Ford previously told the Sun-Times warmer temperatures and increased moisture in the atmosphere can create environments that favor stronger thunderstorms.</p><p>However, researchers say the relationship between climate change and tornadoes themselves remains less certain.</p><p>Ford said a warmer, more humid climate may be contributing to more environments favorable for severe storms, though scientists are still studying exactly how those conditions affect tornado frequency.</p><p><i>Contributing: Mohammad Samra, Elijah James, Brett Chase</i></p>

entries.title: Cubs TV analyst Jim Deshaies toughing it out before hip-replacement surgery
entries.summary: <p>The Cubs’ series this weekend against the Cardinals is one of those that the national networks take over. Apple TV will carry the game Friday, and ABC has the game Sunday.</p><p>But if it were up to Cubs analyst Jim Deshaies, that Friday game would be on Marquee Sports Network.</p><p>“There should be a rule that only we get to do Friday afternoon games,” he said this week. “Unfortunately, that’s not the rule, and Apple can pick up a certain number of games. I love those Friday afternoon games because we’re the only ones that are playing at the time.”</p><p>Indeed, those 1:20 p.m. starts harken back to a time when every Cubs home game was a day game. Lights were installed in 1988, and they’re never coming down. Just as streaming services such as Apple TV aren’t going away.</p><p>“I get it. That’s the nature of the beast, and we’re the Cubs,” Deshaies said. “The national people want to do Cub games because we’re a good draw. But a weekend with the Cardinals, the Air Show in town, I’d probably rather be working than not.”</p><p>The time off will give Deshaies, 66, a break from navigating Wrigley Field on crutches. This spring, he began to feel pain in his left hip, and imaging revealed he needs a new one. Not wanting to miss the season, he’s scheduled for surgery Sept. 30 in Chicago.</p><p>“I was just limping around, kind of dragging my leg for a while,” Deshaies said. “My wife was at a physical therapist for her back and told the therapist what I was doing. They said he should be on crutches to take the heat off that leg. I’m not in a ton of pain. It’s inconvenient, but it’s certainly manageable.”</p><p>The Cubs have managed to play some of their best baseball of the season lately, hopping off the roller coaster they rode before the All-Star break. Deshaies has taken great joy in watching them play defense, particularly center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong, second baseman Nico Hoerner and shortstop Dansby Swanson.</p><p>“I’m always telling [producer Mike Leary] and the boys in the truck, ‘I see a defensive package coming, a montage of defensive plays,’ ” Deshaies said. “And then [replay technician Mitch Nakhshin] will build that in. I love watching the defense do its thing.”</p><p>And Cubs fans love listening to Deshaies, whether he’s with Jon “Boog” Sciambi or Alex Cohen. If you see him around the ballpark, give him room. Although, he must say, “I’m getting pretty good on the crutches.”</p><div class="PageListC" data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Bears will sit QB Caleb Williams vs. Browns in preseason opener, backup Tyson Bagent to start
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> will watch the preseason opener against the Browns on Saturday from the sideline. Backup Tyson Bagent will start and likely play the first half.</p><p>"I don't know that I need to see game snaps," coach Ben Johnson said of Williams. "What were trying to assess is the volume throughout the week and... making sure our team is ready for a 17-game season. Do I need to see Caleb Williams in the preseason? No I see him every day in practice."</p><p>Johnson added that he wants to see Williams and the offense hit certain "benchmarks" of progress, but he also is taking significant input from the training staff with a goal of keeping players' total snaps between practices and games to a reasonable level in order to be fresh for the start of the season Sept. 13 at the Panthers.</p><p>In Williams' case, he said he hasn't decided whether preseason game snaps will be part of the equation. The Bears have preseason games the next two weeks at the Bengals and Titans, plus joint practices against each of those teams ahead of those matchups. Johnson could opt to have Williams get his game-like snaps in those practices.</p><p>Johnson said he also will sit several starters on both sides of the ball, but didn't want to list them all. Behind Bagent, the Bears have third-stringer Case Keenum and undrafted rookie Miller Moss.</p><p>Last season, Johnson held Williams out of the preseason opener against the Dolphins, then played him against the Bills and Chiefs.</p><p>Browns coach Todd Monken, meanwhile, indicated Wednesday he will start veteran Deshaun Watson, then turn to Shedeur Sanders in the second half. Watson and Sanders both are competing for the starting job.</p>

entries.title: Agente de ICE se declara culpable de agresión mientras estaba fuera de servicio
entries.summary: <p>Un agente del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) se declaró culpable el miércoles de un ataque cuando estaba fuera de servicio y que ocurrió a finales del año pasado en una gasolinería en el suburbio de Brookfield.</p><p>Adam Saracco, de 41 años, fue sentenciado a un año de supervisión por la Corte del Circuito del Condado de Cook por un único delito menor de agresión durante una breve audiencia ante el juez Owens J. Shelby.</p><p>Saracco fue acusado a principios de este año después de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/23/ice-officer-charged-with-attacking-immigrant-rights-activist-in-chicago-suburbs" target="_blank" >atacar al abogado y activista Robert Held</a> el 27 de diciembre. Held siguió a Saracco desde la instalación de procesamiento de ICE en Broadview y lo filmó cuando se detuvo en una gasolinería en la cuadra 9200 al este de 31st Street en Brookfield. Held dijo que Saracco finalmente se le acercó y lo empujó al suelo.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e00000" name="module-e00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>"Me satisface que exista cierta rendición de cuentas", dijo Held al Sun-Times. "Pero como país, nos falta mucho por recorrer".</p><p>Held presionó para que la fiscalía del Condado de Cook <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/26/ice-midway-blitz-adam-saracco-robert-held-trump-chicago-brookfield" target="_blank" >elevara el caso de Saracco</a> a un asunto de delito grave, pero los fiscales se negaron tras una revisión.</p><p>Held sostuvo que Saracco debía enfrentar un cargo por delito grave porque el presunto ataque ocurrió en una acera pública y porque Held tiene más de 60 años. Pero los fiscales dijeron que un cargo por delito grave requeriría que demostraran que Saracco sabía que Held tenía más de 60 años y señalaron que rara vez persiguen cargos de agresión agravada basándose únicamente en la ubicación de un presunto ataque.</p><p>No se pudo localizar al abogado de Saracco y tampoco pudo contactarse con ICE para que dieran su versión de los hechos.</p><p>La condena de Saracco ocurre en medio de llamados continuos para responsabilizar a los agentes federales por sus acciones durante el Operativo Midway Blitz, la campaña de deportaciones de la administración de Trump en el área de Chicago ocurrida el otoño pasado. El lunes, residentes entraron en la sede del Área 3 del Departamento de Policía de Chicago en North Center para <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/08/11/marimar-martinez-y-otros-denuncian-a-agentes-del-operativo-midway-blitz-buscando-rendicion-de-cuentas" target="_blank" >denunciar presuntos delitos</a> relacionados con agentes de inmigración.</p><p>La jueza de la Corte del Circuito del Condado de Cook, Erica Reddick, rechazó una petición para nombrar a un fiscal especial que investigara presuntas faltas penales y, potencialmente, procesara a agentes federales. La oficina de la fiscal ha sostenido que las agencias encargadas de hacer cumplir la ley deben investigar los presuntos delitos y presentar los casos a los fiscales para su imputación.</p><p>Ningún agente federal ha sido acusado de cometer un delito en servicio relacionado con el Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>Más tarde el miércoles, la fiscal del Condado de Cook, Eileen O'Neill Burke, dijo, "Nadie está por encima de la ley y eso incluye a los agentes de ICE".</p><p>"Mi oficina se compromete a buscar que se haga justicia en nombre de cualquier persona perjudicada durante el Operativo Midway Blitz cuando la evidencia y la ley nos permitan procesar", dijo O'Neill Burke en un comunicado. "Esta resolución representa un paso importante para la rendición de cuentas y demuestra que el Condado de Cook no se hará de la vista gorda ante conductas ilícitas, sin importar quién seas".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" >La Voz Chicago</a></p>

entries.title: Cubs-White Sox rivalry is missing something — commercials!
entries.summary: <p>You know what the White Sox-Cubs series next week needs?</p><p>A commercial.</p><p>Hear me out.</p><p>As recently as the late aughts, Cubs manager Lou Piniella and Sox skipper Ozzie Guillen appeared in a Chevy commercial around the time of the crosstown series, rapping to their heart’s content.</p><p>Guillen: “I’m a South Side guy.”</p><p>Piniella: “I know, I can tell.”</p><p>Guillen: “What’s that mean? You can go to hell [bleeped by a car horn].”</p><p>Piniella: “Sparks will fly from our Cubbie bats.”</p><p>Guillen: “You remind me of Minnesota Fats.”</p><p>Piniella: “I’m a North Side guy.”</p><p>Guillen: “I know, I can tell.”</p><p>Piniella: “At least I ain’t trapped in no South Side cell [Rate Field was called U.S. Cellular Field].”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/cvaogIfz8mA?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Lou Piniella - Chevy (Cubs Sox Rap) Commercial"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Can you imagine those words coming out of the mouths of current managers Craig Counsell and Will Venable? It’s unfathomable.</p><p>Guillen and Piniella did another commercial for the Chevy Camaro in which they glared at each other from their cars and played chicken until a giant baseball dropped between them.</p><p>It speaks to a different era, before streaming took hold, when we all watched TV and saw Chicago sports figures in local commercials. Now, they only seem to appear in those ubiquitous Akin Law ads.</p><p>For example, when Cubs Hall of Famer Andre Dawson hit a home run over the fence at Wrigley Field, we knew he hit it over a Tru-Link fence because that’s what he said in the commercial.</p><p>But a Cubs-Sox commercial hits different. It attracts everyone. It just needs two managers willing to, well, embarrass themselves for a good laugh. During their rap, Piniella strutted like a peacock with his hands in his back pockets, and Guillen looked like a gangsta rapper.</p><p>Maybe there’s hope for Counsell and Venable. After all, in 1986, the Cubs’ Jim Frey and the Sox’ Tony La Russa put on a good show in a Busch beer commercial before what was then an exhibition game. They talked on the phone while childishly marking up pictures of each other on a Busch display, adding silly mustaches and blacking out teeth.</p><p>La Russa: “Yeah, Jim. You look real good next to it.”</p><p>Frey: “Tony, you never looked better yourself.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/lJ-sxqzKe_o?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="1986 - Jim Frey - Tony La Russa Crosstown Classic Beer Ad"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Never mind that they were fired in June that season, about a week apart.</p><p>Such mockery is part of a rivalry. Even the Bears and Packers exchanged playful McDonald’s commercials in 1990. After the Packers’ Tony Mandarich taunted Bears fans with fries – “Hope you got a lot of potato farmers down there in Illinois,” with emphasis on the S – the Bears’ Dan Hampton did his own version for Packers fans.</p><p>It got a little nasty in the press. Bears coach Mike Ditka called Mandarich a “Bozo.” Replied Mandarich: “Then I’m a $35,000 Bozo.” That’s what McDonald’s paid him.</p><p>How awesome was that?</p><p>In the early 2010s, actors Nick Offerman (Cubs fan) and Craig Robinson (Sox fan) appeared in clever commercials for New Era, arguing with deadpanned faces about baseball topics at the fictional Chicago bar The Dividing Line.</p><p>Robinson: “How old is Wrigley anyway? Do you even have electricity?”</p><p>Offerman: “It’s powered by tradition, my friend. Something you wouldn’t know about at mobile phone park.”</p><p>Funny stuff.</p><p>We need more of that, but from the combatants involved. Put center fielders Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs and Tristan Peters of the Sox, both All-Stars, on a set and let them make fun of each other and each other’s team.</p><p>Such hijinks aren’t coming from managers anymore. Guillen and Piniella had a huge presence. Venable and Counsell do not, and their team owners probably like it that way. They don’t want anyone casting a shadow over the club.</p><p>Even if it makes for entertaining television.</p><div class="PageListC" data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Bears close Thursday's training camp practice to fans
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> closed practice Thursday to fans because of projected inclement weather in the mid-afternoon.</p><p>Practice is scheduled to begin at 12:45 p.m. The team could move it from their outdoor fields to the Walter Payton Center if weather disrupts their practice. Tickets, which are free, are non-transferrable. As was the case for other weather-related cancellations during camp, the Bears offered their fans a coupon at their online store in apology.</p><p>Thursday marked the third training camp practice closed to fans in a 15-day span. On Sunday, fans were forced to leave and practice was delayed and later moved indoors when a lightning storm blew through Lake Forest.</p><p>The Bears are set to begin their preseason slate Saturday against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/12/bears-training-camp-browns-start-deshaun-watson-saturday-shedeur-sanders-nfl" target="_blank" >Browns</a> at Soldier Field. They'll travel to practice in Cincinnati and Nashville in the following two weeks. The opener is Sept. 13 in Charlotte, N.C.<br></p>

entries.title: Experienced No. 6 Oswego eyes a return to the state title game
entries.summary: <p>Oswego is the area’s new high school sports hotbed. Both local schools regularly produce high-level athletes and teams. It isn’t difficult to figure out why. The village in Kendall County has grown from 3,876 residents in 1990 to nearly 40,000 today.</p><p>High school football has always been a focal point of the community. Oswego won the 7A state title in 2003 and a 4A title in 1992. But last season was even bigger, despite <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2025/12/03/mount-carmel-football-chicago-state-title-oswego" >losing the 8A title game to Mount Carmel</a>.</p><p>“The semifinal crowd was unbelievable,” Panthers quarterback Drew Kleinhans said. “I’ve never seen that many people at a high school football game. Some people said it was one of the best games they had ever been to, crowd-wise.”</p><p>The Panthers were the Cinderella story of last season’s state tournament, upsetting Maine South on the road in the quarterfinals and beating Lockport at home in the semifinals. Then they gave heavily-favored Mount Carmel a stern test in the title game.</p><p>Coach Brian Cooney was a linebacker on the 1992 state championship team and an assistant coach with the 2003 team. His tenure as head coach has been stellar, leading Oswego to a 126-36 record in 15 seasons. The Panthers have only missed the playoffs once since 2010.</p><p>All that success has probably been mildly underappreciated across the state. That has changed after last season’s run, and the community is buying in as well.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a the summer are about 180-190. This summer we had well over 200 sign up.”</p><p>Oswego, ranked No. 6 in the preseason Super 25, won’t be sneaking up on anyone this season.</p><p>“We aren’t worried about having a target on our back,” said Iowa State recruit Dontrell Young, a defensive back. “We have pretty high standards and plan to finish things off this year and bring the state championship home.”</p><p>The Panthers return around eight starters on offense and seven on defense. The offensive line, with returners Ryan Stork, Gabriel Guzman, Nathan Overstreet and Alejandro Acosta, should be a major strength.</p><p>Kleinhans threw for 18 TD passes last season, his first on varsity.</p><p>“There were some times last year where the game felt a little fast,” Kleinhans said. “Already this year in practice against our great defense and the scrimmages against Batavia, the game feels a lot slower to me, and everything feels a lot smoother.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-hangRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2a0000" name="module-2a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Oswego schedule</b><br><ul id="rte-1b79d672-9730-11f1-9907-f970875bd4a3"><li><b>Aug. 21</b> vs. Neuqua Valley</li><li><b>Aug. 28</b> at Geneva</li><li><b>Sept. 4</b> vs. Plainfield North</li><li><b>Sept. 11</b> at Bolingbrook</li><li><b>Sept. 18</b> vs. Plainfield South</li><li><b>Sept. 25</b> at Yorkville</li><li><b>Oct. 2</b> at Joliet West</li><li><b>Oct. 9</b> vs. Minooka</li><li><b>Oct. 16</b> at Oswego East</li></ul></div> </div><p>Cooney has been impressed with 6-4 senior tight end Ryan Wynn’s improvement over the offseason, and junior running back Ammar Banire, a part-time player last season, recently earned scholarship offers from eight schools including Illinois, Indiana and Iowa. He will partner with fullback Graham Schwab in a dynamic backfield.</p><p>“We haven’t been listening to any outside noise,” Banire said. “All we did was work harder. This season we have the chip on our shoulder that we can go and win it all.”</p><p>Young, who won three medals at the state track and field meet, leads the defense along with linebacker Cam Loghmani. The 5-10, 205-pound senior finished with 82 tackles and 10 TFLs last season.</p><p>“With more guys back this year, the installs have been a little bit smoother,” Cooney said. “They have been able to pick things up a little bit more, and we have more at our disposal in Week 1. entries.title: White Sox move up start time for series finale vs. Reds
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox moved up the start time for the game Thursday against the Reds one hour to 12:10 p.m. because of the forecast for rain later this afternoon.</p><p>Manager Will Venable said talk about moving the game began in the 9 a.m. hour. The Sox announced the change at 10:10. Venable said for him, this was the closest to first pitch that a game time was moved. </p><p>"But these guys are the best in the world at making adjustments," he said. "So they’ll be ready to go."</p><p>Venable said the late change affected all of the Sox' pregame plans.</p><p>"We had some meetings in place that we had to make adjustments on," he said. "We were going to take ground balls today; weren’t able to do that. A little bit of a scramble, but these guys will be ready to go.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: White Sox pope hat giveaway has some fans cashing in
entries.summary: <p>Thousands of White Sox fans attending Tuesday night's game got to take home a free hat fashioned in honor of team fan Pope Leo XIV. Now, listings for the exclusive pope hat are appearing online for sale. </p><p>Sellers on eBay and Facebook Marketplace are hawking the black-and-gold mitre hat featuring the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> logo. </p><p>One eBay seller is offering the hat for $129.99, and as of Wednesday evening, they've sold 15 hats with four still available. Other listings, advertising the pope hat as a "unique" and "collectible" item, noted their stock as unworn. Most hats found by the Sun-Times were selling between $50 and $100, but it's unclear if all of the hats are authentic.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Hindsight, I feel like the hat is actually more valuable," he said.</p><p>Lipinsky said he has attended about 11 games this season.</p><p>After listing the hat on Facebook, he received 20 responses.</p><p>"I'm selling to [a guy on Facebook]," he said. "I'm meeting him up at Walgreens in, like, 20 minutes."</p><p>He's gotten his fair share of freebies thanks to the team's regular game day promotions. He lines the man cave in his basement with the items, typically Sox bobbleheads, he said. </p><p>White Sox Manager Will Venable said in a statement, “My girls got several pope hats, so there’s a few of them laying around the apartment. It was awesome. It was really cool, the energy in the ballpark. Some of the things in-between innings. It was a really fun night.” </p><p>The giveaway was initially for 2,500 fans purchasing a special ticket package, but was expanded to the entire stadium of nearly 41,000. </p><p>Brooks Boyer, White Sox executive vice president, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/11/white-sox-pope-leo-hat-night" >told the Sun-Times</a> Tuesday that the giveaway caught the attention of the pope, whose brother confirmed to the team’s front office that the pontiff had heard about the event.</p><p>He said Thursday that the pope hat was an item that all fans should have received, compared to its more limited giveaways.</p><p>“We viewed the promotion as a creative way to celebrate one of the franchise’s most popular fans, and by the overwhelming response we received, White Sox fans certainly agreed," Boyer said in a statement.</p><p><i>This story has been updated with comments from the White Sox.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/11/white-sox-pope-leo-hat-night" >White Sox Pope Leo night draws thousands for pontiff hats and Catholic fanfare</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/photography/2026/08/12/white-sox-pope-leo-xiv-rate-field-photos" >PHOTOS: White Sox ‘pope hat’ giveaway brings out faithful fans</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Homeowners continue cleanup after EF-1 tornado ravages neighborhoods in Northwest Indiana
entries.summary: <p>Laura Ramos said she grabbed her cat and hunkered down in her bathtub Tuesday after her phone sounded an alarm warning that a tornado was headed her way.</p><p>Moments later, a tornado with wind gusts of 86 to 110 mph tore through her Munster, Indiana, neighborhood, knocking down power lines, uprooting trees and buckling sidewalks. The National Weather Service confirmed the EF-1 tornado touched down on the north side of town.</p><p>“It’s true what they say that it sounds like a train going over your roof,” said Ramos, 59.</p><p>Indiana Gov. Mike Braun declared a state of emergency Thursday in response to widespread damage in Northwest Indiana from this week’s severe storms that brought flooding and tornadoes to the state. Weather officials also confirmed an EF-2 tornado touched down in St. John, Indiana.</p><p>“Hoosiers’ safety is my top priority,” Braun said in a statement. “Our state response is fully mobilized, resources are moving where they’re needed, and we will continue working around the clock to support every impacted community.”</p><p>Braun also deployed the Indiana National Guard to help communities in Lake County clear tree debris, according to the Lake County Homeland Security and Emergency Management Agency.</p><p>Ramos' home was damaged when the tornado knocked down two of her trees, causing one to land on her house. On Thursday morning, her sister-in-law and brother-in-law drove in from Chicago to help her with the cleanup.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> passed, Ramos said she was overcome with emotion as she surveyed the damage to her neighborhood. She moved into her home in the 8400 block of Moraine Avenue in 2009 and said she barely recognized the area after the storm.</p><p>“I made the mistake of going on a walk around the block, and I broke down and cried because everybody’s front yards were flipped over,” she said.</p><p>Though she suffered damage to her roof, Ramos said it could have been much worse.</p><p>On Thursday afternoon, several of Ramos’ neighbors were seen sawing through fallen trees and raking up leaves and debris. The steady hum of generators could also be heard as residents worked to keep their homes powered.</p><p>Ramos said she only had a small generator with enough power to charge her cellphone.</p><p>Thousands remained without power Thursday after the severe storms knocked out service for a majority of customers.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.nipsco.com/" target="_blank" ><u>NIPSCO</u></a> said late Thursday morning it had restored service for 75,000 of the 313,000 electric customers who lost service. The utility service said it was the largest outage event in its history.</p><p>It was unclear how long it would take to restore power. Many residents in Munster and Hammond said they were prepared to remain without electricity through at least the weekend, while some expected the outages to last even longer.</p><div entries.title: White Sox starter Davis Martin ejected after hitting Reds' Sal Stewart with pitch
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox </a>right-hander Davis Martin was ejected in the third inning after knocking off Reds first baseman Sal Stewart's helmet with a pitch, prompting both dugouts and bullpens to empty. Stewart had hit a 419-foot homer off Martin in the first, but Martin's control had been off.</p><p>Martin had hit Reds catcher Tyler Stephenson in the first and had hit the backstop with several pitches. With the count 0-1 to Stewart, Martin sailed his next pitch over Stewart's head. The following pitch grazed the bill of Stewart's helmet, knocked it off. Stewart held the barrel of the bat and pointed the knob at Martin, then held up two fingers, indicating that Martin had come up and in twice.</p><p>That's when the benches and bullpens emptied, but no punches were thrown. Though Martin had not been warned, the umpires ejected him. Manager Will Venable came out to argue, but to no avail.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Davis Martin has been ejected from today's game vs. the Cincinnati Reds.<br><br>Erick Fedde is now in the game. <a href="https://t.co/O3PKtnlCdK">pic.twitter.com/O3PKtnlCdK</a></p>— White Sox on CHSN (@CHSN_WhiteSox) <a href="https://x.com/CHSN_WhiteSox/status/2087962169962807537?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 13, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Hunting season begins early on for Bulls with 2026-27 schedule release
entries.summary: <p>Dailyn Swain wasn’t trying to manufacture phony hype.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls’</a> first-year guard was simply stating facts.</p><p>Minutes after he watched rookie teammate Caleb Wilson make it a point to go after fellow top draft pick Cameron Boozer in their first Summer League head-to-head matchup since their Duke-North Carolina showdowns, Swain was only reiterating the obvious.</p><p>After all, Wilson had been very boisterous in how he planned to chase down Rookie of the Year honors this upcoming season, and if that meant running down — and going over — the competition, so be it.</p><p>“You know what happened when I played them (in the 2025-26 college season), so I don’t really care about the media,” Wilson said last month when discussing his No. 4 draft selection and the three players that went in front of him. “I’m a competitor … whatever needs to be done to prove I’m on the same level … but I’m better.”</p><p>That was the point Swain was making recently. That Wilson is not only from the school of talking it but took night classes on walking it.</p><p>“I mean Caleb is hunting everybody,” Swain said. “He won’t say it enough, but we can see it in his mentality, pregame, during the game, like he’s hunting these (other rookies). He works so hard. I’m not surprised by it. Guys like him are just like that.”</p><p>They are. So while the Bulls announced the regular-season schedule on Thursday, opening up the 2026-27 campaign in Toronto on Oct. 21, the home opener is three nights later against Washington and No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa. Or as far as Wilson was concerned, that’s when hunting season starts.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>THE TOP FIVE MOST INTERESTING GAMES/MOMENTS:</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p><b>Wizards at Bulls – Oct. 24: </b>Yes, it will be the home opener for the new-look Bulls, from front office, to coaching staff, to half the roster. But that’s only the subplot. Washington has high hopes for the year with the additions of Trae Young and Anthony Davis, along with Dybantsa and the likes of young talent such as Alex Sarr and Kyshawn George.</p><p>Not only will this be a measuring stick for the Bulls and the battle for possible turnaround teams in the Eastern Conference, but the Wilson vs. Dybantsa matchup is can’t miss TV.</p><p></p><p><b>Three weeks of hell – Oct. 26 through Nov. 16: </b>If the Bulls have any hopes of a quick start out of the gate, they might want to check those. Starting right after the home debut against the Wizards, the Bulls will go on a three-week juggernaut that will quickly test new coach Tiago Splitter and the roster that Bryson Graham has constructed.</p><p>In that time, they will play in Boston twice, a home and home with the world champion New York Knicks, a home and home with LeBron James and the Philadelphia 76ers, the Western Conference champs in San Antonio, as well as matchups with playoff bound Atlanta, Minnesota and Cleveland.</p><p><b>Bulls at Hornets – Nov. 25: </b>What better way for the Bulls players to get ready for a small Thanksgiving break than by testing themselves against the up-and-coming Hornets, as well as a nice family reunion with long-time guard Coby White?</p><p><b>Bulls at Nuggets – Feb. 11: </b>Not only will the young Bulls start a four-game West Coast trip against MVP-candidate Nikola Jokic in Denver but will do so on trade deadline day. The players that get on the airplane for the start of that trip could very well be calling for their belongings in cardboard boxes by the time the team travels to Portland a few nights later.</p><p></p><p><b>Grizzlies at Bulls – March 13: </b>Boozer is the early leader in the Vegas odds to win Rookie of the Year, and the March tilt will be the first of two meetings Wilson will have against his former ACC foe. entries.title: Bears training camp report No. 13: Injuries linger at key spots in starting lineup
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ Thursday training camp practice:</p><h3><b>What happened</b></h3><p>It was a relatively light day for the Bears as rain drizzled and practice moved indoors midway through when lightning struck near Halas Hall.</p><p>Quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>, who won’t play Saturday against the Browns, was up and down in the few times he threw. There were several drops, including one by wide receiver Rome Odunze up the sideline and another by running back Kyle Monangai in the flats, but also one by linebacker T.J. Edwards on a would-be interception against Williams. Edwards and Williams laughed about the play afterward, with Williams appearing to acknowledge that Edwards surprised him by cutting into his throwing lane.</p><p>Backup quarterback Tyson Bagent, who will start Saturday, closed practice with a deep shot to wide receiver Kaden Davis for a touchdown.</p><h3><b>Position battle</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson hoped to have some clarity at left tackle by now, but that’s been hard to get with leader Braxton Jones sidelined by a knee injury. Jones went through the early part of practice before leaving, and the Bears plan to start Kiran Amegadjie against the Browns, followed by Jedrick Wills.</p><h3><b>Injury watch</b></h3><h3></h3><p>While Johnson has maintained these are relatively minor injuries, defensive end Montez Sweat and cornerbacks Tyrique Stevenson, Jaylon Jones and Terell Smith didn’t practice.</p><h3><b>What’s next?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Bears likely will have their starters go through warmups or some other workout Saturday morning at Soldier Field, then leave the game itself mostly to the reserves. They’ll get the starters back in action at practice Sunday afternoon.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Universidades de Illinois en alerta tras anularse la cuota de inscripción estatal para estudiantes indocumentados
entries.summary: <p>Miles de estudiantes inmigrantes que asistieron a la escuela secundaria en Illinois podrían pronto tener que pagar tarifas de para no residentes más altas en la universidad, un cambio que podría poner en riesgo su acceso a la educación superior.</p><p>El 24 de julio, un juez federal designado por el presidente Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/2b/57/27b24572418b89ce553d526f2a18/gov-uscourts-ilsd-106533-49-0.pdf" target="_blank" >anuló partes de tres leyes de Illinois</a> que permitían a estudiantes indocumentados elegibles pagar las cuotas de inscripción para residentes en los colegios comunitarios y universidades públicas y recibir ayuda financiera estatal.</p><p>El juez David Dugan, de la Corte del Distrito Sur de Illinois, falló a favor del Departamento de Justicia en su argumento de que esas disposiciones violan la ley federal porque otorgan un beneficio a personas no ciudadanas que residen en el estado, beneficio que los ciudadanos que viven fuera del estado no pueden obtener.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7d0000" name="module-7d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La ley estatal <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=60&GAID=3&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=195&SessionID=3&GA=93" target="_blank" >sobre la cuota de inscripción para residentes del estado</a> había estado vigente por más de dos décadas. Para calificar para ese beneficio, los estudiantes deben haber asistido a una escuela secundaria de Illinois por lo menos tres años, entre otros criterios.</p><p>Dugan suspendió la ejecución del fallo por dos semanas para dar tiempo a los funcionarios estatales a apelar, pero no está claro si lo harán. Grupos por los derechos de los inmigrantes como la <a class="Link" href="http://facebook.com/ICIRR/" target="_blank" >Coalición por los Derechos de los Inmigrantes y Refugiados de Illinois</a> (ICIRR) temen que una apelación pueda revertir las políticas de cuota de inscripción para residentes en contra de estudiantes indocumentados en todo el país. Ya, la Universidad Estatal de Illinois, una de las demandadas en el caso, decidió no impugnar la decisión, según <a class="Link" href="https://www.wglt.org/local-news/2026-08-05/federal-court-blocks-in-state-tuition-rates-and-financial-aid-for-undocumented-college-students-in-illinois" target="_blank" >informó WGLT</a>.</p><p>ICIRR estima que entre 7,000 y 10,000 estudiantes indocumentados “podrían perder apoyo educativo vital para el próximo año académico como resultado directo de este fallo”, dijo Verónica Castro, subdirectora de la organización, en un comunicado. “Las familias tendrán que tomar decisiones financieras difíciles, y las tasas de inscripción pueden verse afectadas, lo que representa un gran retroceso para nuestras comunidades”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" La organización estima que entre 7,000 y 10,000 estudiantes indocumentados podrían perder el apoyo en el próximo año escolar debido a la decisión de una corte federal.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Archivo Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Peggy Heinrich, presidenta de Elgin Community College, dijo que el fallo elimina “una fuente fundamental de ayuda” que ha permitido a estudiantes indocumentados “recibir educación y convertirse en miembros productivos y contribuyentes de nuestra sociedad”.</p><p>El colegio comunitario está designado por el gobierno federal como parte de las Instituciones al Servicio de los Hispanos (HSI) y más de la mitad de sus estudiantes se identifican como hispanos o latinos.</p><p>Heinrich dijo que su colegio y otros en Illinois están buscando orientación de los funcionarios estatales sobre lo que significa el fallo.</p><p>“Tenemos que cumplir, por lo que estamos intentando hacer lo mejor posible para asegurarnos de que nuestros estudiantes entiendan qué recursos podrían estar disponibles para ellos, o qué podemos ofrecer en términos de opciones de planes de pago del colegio”, destacó Heinrich.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.higheredimmigrationportal.org/state/illinois/" target="_blank" >Casi 25,000 estudiantes</a> en colegios y universidades de Illinois son indocumentados, según el Higher Ed Immigration Portal, que hace seguimiento de los datos de inscripción de estudiantes inmigrantes en todo el país.</p><p>En muchas universidades, la diferencia entre las cuotas de inscripción para residentes y para no residentes es sustancial. En la Universidad de Illinois en Chicago (UIC), <a class="Link" href="https://uofi.app.box.com/s/3ub3lw8qeda73k7u9bl2927o66vhyvzq" target="_blank" >la cuota de inscripción para no residentes es casi el triple</a> del precio de lo que es para residentes a tiempo completo de pregrado.</p><p>El University of Illinois System, que supervisa UIC, la Universidad de Illinois en Springfield y la Universidad de Illinois en Urbana-Champaign, <a class="Link" href="https://today.uic.edu/important-update-regarding-recent-federal-court-ruling/" target="_blank" >dijo a los estudiantes en un correo electrónico el 3 de agosto</a> que los administradores universitarios están trabajando con funcionarios estatales y abogados para evaluar las implicaciones del fallo.</p><p>“Nuestra prioridad inmediata es proporcionar información precisa y ofrecer orientación y apoyo oportunos a medida que haya más detalles disponibles”, escribieron los administradores.</p><p>Ya no está disponible la solicitud que los estudiantes indocumentados en todo Illinois habrían presentado para recibir ayuda financiera estatal, conocida como la Solicitud Alternativa de Ayuda Financiera de Illinois.</p><p>“Esto significa que los estudiantes que hayan presentado o planeen presentar la Solicitud Alternativa 2026-27, como los estudiantes indocumentados de Illinois, no pueden ser considerados para este programa para el año escolar 2026-27”, señala un <a class="Link" href="https://www.isac.org/students/during-college/types-of-financial-aid/grants/monetary-award-program/" target="_blank" >aviso sobre el fallo</a> de la Comisión de Asistencia Estudiantil de Illinois.</p><p>Se estima que 2,150 estudiantes indocumentados recibieron ayuda financiera estatal a través de uno de los programas de la agencia durante el año escolar 2025-2026, dijo un portavoz. Eso incluye becas MAP para estudiantes de bajos ingresos.</p><p>ICIRR aconsejó a los estudiantes que guarden copias de sus cartas de adjudicación de ayuda financiera, facturas de cuotas de inscripción y los comunicados de su colegio o universidad, y que consulten con sus asesores académicos o con las oficinas de ayuda financiera o admisiones.</p><p>La organización ofreció una sesión informativa para estudiantes y familias sobre el fallo <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/share/v/199RSt1y4b/" target="_blank" >en Facebook Live</a> el miércoles en colaboración con el Latino Policy Forum.</p><p><i>Lisa Kurian Philip cubre educación superior para WBEZ en colaboración con </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampusmedia.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Open Campus</i></a><i>. </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Mike Quigley says he's 'willing to risk the job to save the city' if elected mayor
entries.summary: <p>Chicago needs a mayor who is willing to “risk the job to save the city,” U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley said Thursday, portraying himself as the only candidate in the crowded field willing to “risk it all.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/01/07/us-rep-mike-quigley-mayoral-run-2027-brandon-johnson" >Quigley’s decision to run for mayor</a> and re-election to Congress simultaneously looks more like playing it safe than risking it all. But the 17-year veteran North Side congressman claims the opposite is true.</p><p>If elected mayor, Quigley said it would be his last stop in politics. He would never seek another elected office.</p><p>“The next mayor has to be willing to risk the job to save the city… You have to be willing to say, `This is going to be my last job.’ You have to be willing to risk it all, because we’re out of runway,” Quigley told the Sun-Times. “This is my last and biggest fight. I have nothing to lose. I’m only in this race for Chicago."</p><p>Quigley said his laser focus on government — not politics — will give him freedom to make the politically unpopular decisions required to solve the city’s enormous financial problems.</p><p>Chicago has a $90 million mid-year budget shortfall, a $1 billion gap in next year’s budget and a $36 billion pension crisis that will be made $11 billion worse by the police and fire pension sweetener signed by Gov. JB Pritzker. Police, Fire and Municipal Employees pension funds are hovering dangerously close to insolvency. The city's bond rating is just one level above junk status.</p><p>Quigley acknowledged that the pension protection clause in the Illinois Constitution includes an ironclad guarantee that existing benefits “shall not be diminished or impaired.”</p><p>But there’s nothing stopping the next mayor from asking union leaders to voluntarily make some of the changes needed to save their pensions.</p><p>Quigley promised to do just that.</p><p>“What the mayor has to do… is to say to our union partners, `We’re not gonna take away your pension, but it will fail,’” Quigley said.</p><p>“You call the unions in and tell them,`I want you to come to this meeting and I want the word `yes’ in your vocabulary… If we don’t make some honest trade-offs” — including “how much people pay in, when they start collecting” — then a “slight blip in the economy” could jeopardize their retirement checks altogether.</p><p>“We can meet in rooms and talk about this and negotiate and make it as fair and equitable as we can or, at some point, a federal judge will make these decisions. And we have to remember the federal judge in Detroit said, `I have to treat [pension] debt like any other debt’" that must be paid, he said.</p><p>Quigley said he would confront the city’s budget crisis with the employee layoffs that incumbent Mayor Brandon Johnson has refused to consider for fear of alienating the unions that put him in office. He vowed to eliminate thousands of city jobs and restore the city payroll to pre-pandemic levels, “and then some.”</p><p>His tough-love message to unionized city employees extends to building trade unions that have helped Illinois Secretary of State <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/08/02/alexi-giannoulias-chicago-mayor-candidate-2027-february-election-secretary-of-state" >Alexi Giannoulias, the presumed frontrunner </a>in the crowded race for mayor, amass a $22 million campaign war chest that triples the combined total of the other candidates.</p><p>Quigley promises to build 50,000 affordable housing units over four years and cut the cost of each unit by paying tradespeople a reduced “residential prevailing wage” for single family homes and smaller housing projects.</p><p>“Our goal is to provide affordable housing, which is critical for safety and generational wealth for people who have never had that,” Quigley said. <br>“Unions in 43 states, [including] progressive states like New York and California, have that residential rate. I think the unions would understand that.”</p><p>Johnson struggled to pass his first three budgets and has spent the last three and a half years fighting with a City Council more independent than it has ever been. Quigley says he would embrace that independence, in part by supporting a city charter that gives the City Council a greater role in decision-making.</p><p>“I want the next mayor to have less power because, if you go into it with the other attitude, you fall into the trap that the last couple mayors have had — and that is open, constant friction with the City Council," Quigley said. “My attitude is, when an alder votes the other way, you should pat him [or her] on the back and say, `I hope you’re with me next time.’"</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-8d0000" name="html-embed-module-8d0000"></a> <iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_73d105a8-7855-495c-b1ba-a1114673e5a6&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml" style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Cubs creeping closer to Brewers in NL Central race with 40 games to play until postseason fun begins
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON — It couldn’t have been too happy of a flight home for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/13/after-two-big-nights-showed-bats-potential-cubs-nearly-no-hit-in-battle-of-baseballs-top-offenses" >a shutout loss</a> Thursday in the nation’s capital.</p><p>But a look at the standings ought to have them feeling all right.</p><p>They woke up Thursday just three games back of the division lead in the NL Central, having taken advantage of the rival Brewers getting swept this week in San Diego.</p><p>It’s as close as the Cubs had been since late May, the race constricting with just 40 games remaining on their regular-season schedule.</p><p>That’s still a lot of race to run, and a lot can happen.</p><p>But the way this team has played this summer, the postseason looks like its October destination, and a lengthy stay could be in store for a group that’s had winning a World Series on the mind since getting together in Arizona six months ago.</p><p>Before they can start shifting focus to the postseason, though, there are 40 games to play.</p><p>“It’s no different than when we started spring training, where we were a month ago or where we are today. Today is the only thing that matters,” lefty starter <b>Matthew Boyd</b> said Thursday. “It’s fine to look and believe in where we want to go. We know where we want to go. We know where we can go and what we’re able to do. There’s no limit on that.</p><p>“However, having those thoughts — which are natural, and they will happen, because there’s excitement behind it — you always have to bring it back to what’s expected of you in this moment. That’s the balance, understanding, ‘This is where I’ve got to be right now.’</p><p>“You can think about [the end goal], but you’ve got to come back to what’s important right now and attack that.”</p><h3><b>Gausman’s clunker</b></h3><p>Trade-deadline acquisition <b>Kevin Gausman</b>’s first two starts in a Cubs uniform bookended the team’s 4-2 road trip through Kansas City and Washington, though the second was a far cry from the first.</p><p>Gausman couldn’t get out of the fifth inning Thursday, allowing six runs on seven hits and a walk. That fifth inning unraveled on him, as he allowed four runs with two outs.</p><p>“I couldn’t stop the bleeding,” he said after the game. “I wasn’t good enough to get through six today.”</p><p>He wasn’t good enough to get through five, in actuality, but his mention of a six-inning goal reflects part of the reason the Cubs traded for him, to pitch deep into games and dominate as a top-of-the-rotation arm.</p><p>That’s what they got in his first start, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/07/cubs-kevin-gausman-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-mlb-trade-deadline-royals-blue-jays" >a seven-inning, two-run performance</a> against the Royals, but against the Nationals’ best-in-baseball offense, things didn’t go so hot.</p><p>Though Cubs brass wasn’t sweating this year’s elevated ERA — now up to 4.53 after posting a collective 3.48 mark in the previous four seasons — they’re surely hoping his next turn looks a lot more like Start No. 1 than Start No. 2.</p><h3><b>Miller right</b></h3><p>Righty reliever <b>Shelby Miller</b> struck out all three batters he faced in a minor league rehab outing Wednesday with Double-A Knoxville.</p><p>Miller is still weeks away from a potential return to the big league mound, but his recovery from elbow surgery has impressed the Cubs, who signed him uncertain if he’d be able to pitch at all in 2026.</p><p>“Shelby’s just getting started,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Thursday. “The key, anytime guys are coming off the big surgeries, it’s not necessarily the outings you worry about, it’s the recovery between the outings that you think about the most. Making sure that continues to go well is the priority.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true"
