entries.title: Ex-assessor's office employee avoids prison after cooperating with feds in bribery probe
entries.summary: <p>A man who once worked for the<b> </b>Cook County assessor’s office<b> </b>has become the latest person to avoid prison after being caught up in a bribery scandal — but only after he spent eight years helping the feds and recorded hundreds of conversations, according to his lawyers.</p><p>U.S. District Judge John<b> </b>Kness<b> </b>on Thursday<b> </b>sentenced<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2022/7/6/23197461/lavdim-deme-memisovski-amarjeet-bhachu-cook-county-assessor-property-assessments-tax-bills" target="_blank" >Lavdim<b> </b>Memisovski</a><b> </b>to 18 months<b> </b>of probation. He did so after prosecutors<b> </b>said<b> </b>Memisovski’s<b> </b>assistance<b> </b>had been “integral”<b> </b>to securing several felony convictions<b> </b>tied to wrongdoing in the assessor’s office.</p><p>Still, the judge told Memisovski that “public corruption is … endemic in this district. … It occurs because of individuals like you who hold positions of authority and abuse those positions of authority. Everybody else who didn’t have an ‘in’ had to pay their taxes.”</p><p>The conduct generally dates back to the tenure of former Cook County Assessor Joseph<b> </b>Berrios, who has not been accused by the feds of wrongdoing.</p><p>“I want to apologize to the court for everything that I did. I take full responsibility,” Memisovski said through tears Thursday. “I’ve worked tirelessly to get out of this. It’s just something that I have to deal with.”</p><p>Thursday’s sentencing comes almost<b> </b>exactly<b> </b>four years<b> </b>after<b> </b>Memisovski<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/8/4/23292073/former-cook-county-assessor-worker-pleads-guilty-helped-lower-taxes-exchange-home-improvements" target="_blank" >pleaded guilty<b> </b>to a conspiracy</a> and admitted<b> </b>he’d helped<b> </b>lower taxes<b> </b>on certain Cook County properties<b> </b>by at least $1 million<b> </b>in exchange for personal benefits, like<b> </b>home improvements.</p><p>He did so by lowering<b> </b>property<b> </b>assessments, which are a key factor in calculating property tax bills.</p><p>“[Memisovski’s] scheme gave honest taxpayers good reason to doubt the system: The well-off and connected, who could help fund [Memisovski’s] lifestyle, got an inside track at the Assessor’s Office,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Richard<b> </b>Rothblatt wrote in a recent<b> </b>court memo.</p><p>Still, defense attorney Lisa<b> </b>Wood<b> </b>argued<b> </b>that the assessor's office “had a culture of top-down corruption since long before Mr. Memisovski’s offenses.” She said Memisovski<b> </b>agreed<b> </b>to cooperate with the FBI<b> </b>the day<b> </b>he was approached<b> </b>in July 2018, “wiring up that very day.”</p><p>She said he recorded<b> </b>97<b> </b>meetings<b> </b>and<b> </b>more<b> </b>than<b> </b>400<b> </b>phone calls, even recording armed<b> </b>individuals<b> </b>who<b> </b>“claimed to have connections to organized crime.”<b> </b>His cooperation even led to rifts in his family as he “corroborated the criminal conduct of his own cousin, Lumni Likovski,”<b> </b>she wrote in a separate memo.</p><p>Many of the people he helped prosecute wound up avoiding prison, though. The feds ultimately<b> </b>dropped the charges<b> </b>against<b> </b>Likovski<b> </b>after<b> </b>a co-defendant, Robert<b> </b>Mitziga, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2024/08/06/indiana-businessman-not-guilty-bribing-cook-county-assessor-officials-free-golf" target="_blank" >acquitted<b> </b>at trial</a>. Another co-defendant in that case, Basilio<b> </b>Clausen, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/05/27/ex-cook-county-assessors-employee-gets-probation-after-admitting-to-bribery-scheme-helping-feds" target="_blank" >got<b> </b>three years of probation</a>.</p><p>Another former<b> </b>assessor’s office employee, Francisco<b> </b>Perez, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/07/29/former-cook-county-assessors-official-gets-probation-after-helping-with-feds-lengthy-probe" target="_blank" >got<b> </b>two years of probation</a>. So did John<b> </b>Bodendorfer, who<b> </b>worked for<b> </b>a construction company<b> </b>owned by<b> </b>another player in the scheme.</p><p>But Kness<b> </b>in 2024<b> </b>gave<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2024/08/14/lemont-businessman-sentenced-to-5-years-in-federal-prison-in-conspiracy-to-lower-property-taxes" target="_blank" >a<b> </b>five-year<b> </b>prison sentence<b> </b>to<b> </b>Alex<b> </b>Nitchoff</a>, who<b> </b>owned<b> </b>the construction company where<b> </b>Bodendorfer<b> </b>worked.</p><p>Rothblatt noted that, unlike Memisovski, “Nitchoff did not cooperate with law enforcement officials,”<b> </b>and the benefit to his companies “was substantial.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2022/7/6/23197461/lavdim-deme-memisovski-amarjeet-bhachu-cook-county-assessor-property-assessments-tax-bills" target="_blank" >Cook County assessor’s official charged in corruption case with taking home improvements, jewelry to help cut taxes</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/8/4/23292073/former-cook-county-assessor-worker-pleads-guilty-helped-lower-taxes-exchange-home-improvements" target="_blank" >Ex-Cook County assessor worker admits he helped cut taxes by $1M in exchange for home improvements</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2024/08/14/lemont-businessman-sentenced-to-5-years-in-federal-prison-in-conspiracy-to-lower-property-taxes" target="_blank" >Lemont businessman sentenced to 5 years in federal prison in conspiracy to lower property taxes</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Man critically injured in Humboldt Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was critically injured in a shooting in Humboldt Park Thursday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 24, was shot in the chest and found in the 600 North Spaulding Avenue at 1:30 p.m., police said in a statement. He was taken in critical condition to Stroger Hospital and was stabilized, police said.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said.</p>

entries.title: Driver 'just went through' pedestrian in fatal Lake View hit-and-run, witness says
entries.summary: <p>A man charged with drunk driving in a fatal crash allegedly didn't stop for a pedestrian crossing the road in Lake View and "just went through her," a witness told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Sarah Milcarek, 25, was thrown in the air and crashed through the vehicle's rear windshield, landing in its backseat, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/11/motorist-flees-causes-multiple-crashes-in-fatal-lake-view-hit-and-run" target="_blank" >according to prosecutors</a>. The vehicle kept going and crashed into another car, then a tree. Milcarek had been trying to cross the street from between two cars in the 1400 block of West Irving Park Road on Saturday.</p><p>“She didn’t do anything wrong. She looked both ways,” witness Liam Schalosy, 30, of Logan Square, told the Sun-Times. “We all thought he was either gonna slam his brakes, or he was gonna swerve out of the way. But he just went through her.”</p><p>Schalosy had been driving with his wife when he noticed a driver behind him speeding. He noticed that the driver was going too quickly for her to get out of the way. </p><p>After the crash, Schalosy's wife rushed to the smoke coming from the car that had crashed into a tree, but the driver was nowhere to be found. Bystanders found and tackled the alleged driver, Miroslaw Ciszek, 34, as he tried to walk away, but he broke free, prosecutors said. Police allegedly found him three hours later in a nearby park. A blood test seven hours after the crash measured above the legal limit at .088, prosecutors said. Meanwhile, Milcarek was pronounced dead at a hospital.</p><p>Schalosy said what happened has been on his mind ever since, though he was glad to see the alleged driver was arrested.</p><p>“It brought me a bit of peace that at least he got caught — he got charged,” Schalosy said.</p><p>A judge on Tuesday released Ciszek on electronic monitoring.</p>

entries.title: After two big nights showed bats’ potential, Cubs nearly no-hit in battle of baseball’s top offenses
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON — It’s been more than a month since the big 250th-anniversary celebration in the nation’s capital.</p><p>But the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> and Nationals still provided plenty of fireworks in this week’s battle between the two highest-scoring teams in baseball.</p><p>Of course, the baseball gods hate a narrative, and after scoring 20 runs in back-to-back wins in the first two games of the series, the Cubs went quiet in Thursday’s 7-0 loss. It was the other end of the spectrum from a 12-run, four-homer output the night before, with Nationals right-hander Cade Cavalli taking a no-hit bid into the seventh inning.</p><p>The bloop hit off the bat of first baseman Michael Busch’s bat isn’t the kind of offensive highlight these Cubs have cooked up during a summer in which they’ve been one of the sport’s best teams, but it will be replayed as the knock that made sure Cole Hamels’ gem from 11 years ago is still the most recent no-no against the franchise.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Michael Busch breaks up Cade Cavalli's no-no in the seventh.<br><br>There has not been a single-pitcher no-hitter in MLB since Blake Snell on August 2, 2024 <a href="https://t.co/lgeLNTdasK">pic.twitter.com/lgeLNTdasK</a></p>— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) <a href="https://x.com/TalkinBaseball_/status/2088022325992001883?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 13, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Nationals scored just one fewer run over the three days, with 19 that ensured the Cubs won’t catch their major league lead just yet. The two teams combined for 13 home runs in the series.</p><p>Even with Thursday’s outage, though, the Cubs still possess a potent lineup that seems primed to do damage come October, and they looked like it this week.</p><p>“It’s a really fun group to be around, super talented,” righty pitcher Kevin Gausman said. “The offense, the last two days, we’ve seen what they’re capable of.”</p><p>What they’re capable of is getting a big performance from any one of their hitters on any given night.</p><p>Wednesday, it was third baseman Alex Bregman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/12/cubs-alex-bregman-three-homers-dansby-swanson-ryan-rolison-phil-maton-knee-injury-jackson-kent-nationals" >with three home runs and seven RBIs</a>, adding to his increasingly excellent second-half production that’s vaulted him into the group of Cubs hitters who can win big games by themselves, joining the likes of center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong, right fielder Seiya Suzuki, left fielder Ian Happ and shortstop Dansby Swanson, among others.</p><p>“That’s why this is a good team, because we have a different guy who can do something like that any day,” manager Craig Counsell said Wednesday. “Dansby has done it. Pete’s certainly done it. Ian’s done it. Seiya’s done it. It’s pretty cool.”</p><p>“We’ve got a lot of good players,” Swanson said, “a lot of guys that have been successful in this league for a lot of time now, guys that are prepared and go about their business the right way, guys that take at-bats with the team in mind, going up there to compete. When you’ve got nine guys doing that, it makes it really tough.”</p><p>For a Cubs team questing for a championship at October’s end, this offense is more than just capable, it’s something that can tilt the scales in their favor, including against the type of top-of-the-line competition they’ll face in the postseason.</p><p>Cavalli might not be a big name like Paul Skenes or Tarik Skubal — the two reigning Cy Young winners who took losses against the Cubs in the last few weeks — but he’s having a mighty fine season, lowering his ERA to 3.36 with eight shutout innings Thursday.</p><p>But see the 22 runs the Cubs scored in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/05/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-shohei-ohtani-nl-mvp-race-dodgers-playoffs-craig-counsell-shota-imanaga" >a three-game sweep of the juggernaut Dodgers</a> last week.</p><p>They’ve been good enough that Thursday’s shutout was just their fourth in their last 70 games. Even after getting blanked, they’re averaging 5.8 runs a game this month.</p><p>“We have a very complete batting order. We have a very complete bench. We don’t have any weak spots,” lefty pitcher Matthew Boyd said. “Our lineup is deep, and we have the ability to score runs, regardless of who the pitcher is. We are able to score in a variety of ways, which is really, really special, too. … There’s always trust in this offense that whether it’s two runs or six, we have the ability to come back.”</p><p>“It’s unbelievable,” lefty pitcher David Peterson said. “It feels like we’re never out of a game”</p><p>Unless, of course, they don’t get any hits at all, or just one pop up that drops in the right spot.</p><p>But hey, that’s the baseball gods for you.</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Loop data center pitched for landmarked office building
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago investor’s plan to convert part of a landmark Loop office building into a data center received its first city approval last week, a move Chicago’s leading preservationist group called “a dangerous precedent.”</p><p>Igor Gabal is pitching the conversion of the second through sixth floors of 300 W. Adams St. into a data center, with a new ComEd vault to power it. Ten backup generators would also be installed on the building’s roof.</p><p>The Commission on Chicago Landmarks' Permit Review Committee approved the project on Aug. 6, though the full commission still has to green light the plan.</p><p>An affiliate of Gabal purchased 300 W. Adams St. for $4 million in 2023, property records show. Gabal said during the meeting that he’s tried to find new tenants but “no one wants to lease space” in Class C buildings like the Adams Street property, especially amid a period when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/work/2025/09/26/more-office-workers-revive-loop-but-office-vacancy-rate-still-high" >office vacancy rates remain elevated</a> following the pandemic. Instead, tenants are flocking to Class A buildings, which boast modern finishes and amenities like gyms and coffee shops.</p><p>The 1927 building was nearly 60% vacant as of 2023, according to the Permit Review Committee.</p><p>Gabal didn’t respond to a request for comment.</p><p>If approved, his plans to consolidate existing office tenants into the building’s upper floors, in addition to infilling the light court on the third through fifth floors. The ComEd vault would replace a retail space on the ground floor, with three additional retail spaces remaining available. Gabal’s team said the first floor is the only space where the vault could fit, given its size and proximity to incoming power.</p><p>He said the vault would be no more than 50 megawatts — considerably less than large hyperscale data centers, whose energy use can go up to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/12/16/illinois-pritzker-energy-needs-nuclear-gas-power-plants-climate-change-renewable" >hundreds of megawatts</a>. The building’s <a class="Link" href="https://stack.inspacexr.com/projects/mdi-access/300-w-by-chilled-ai#information" target="_blank" >brochure</a> advertises the “new medium-voltage vault” as 20.4 megawatts.</p><p>Committee staff said during last week's meeting that Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) reviewed the proposal and had no objections. They also acknowledged that, despite rising and “valid” concerns over data centers, their purview is solely from the perspective of historic buildings. </p><p>With a few tweaks to Gabal’s plan — including setting data center equipment 3 feet away from all historic windows — staff said the project fit the guidelines for altering historic buildings.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f60000" name="image-f60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/95e29ef/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5938x3333+0+465/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Feb%2Fde%2F464774c941daa3073a8e38e9659d%2Fadams-260814-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d038a9b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5938x3333+0+465/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Feb%2Fde%2F464774c941daa3073a8e38e9659d%2Fadams-260814-3.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2563044/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5938x3333+0+465/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Feb%2Fde%2F464774c941daa3073a8e38e9659d%2Fadams-260814-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The entrance and lower facade of 300 W. Adams St." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2563044/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5938x3333+0+465/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Feb%2Fde%2F464774c941daa3073a8e38e9659d%2Fadams-260814-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/62a9b0b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5938x3333+0+465/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Feb%2Fde%2F464774c941daa3073a8e38e9659d%2Fadams-260814-3.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2563044/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5938x3333+0+465/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Feb%2Fde%2F464774c941daa3073a8e38e9659d%2Fadams-260814-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The entrance and lower facade of 300 W. Adams St.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Data centers have drawn fire in Chicago and across the country because of their potential to negatively affect the environment, drain water supplies and drive up energy costs. Mayor Brandon Johnson cited those impacts Tuesday when he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/11/mayor-brandon-johnson-chicago-moratorium-data-centers-new-regulations" >signed an executive order</a> establishing regulatory guardrails strengthening the city’s approach toward data center development. He also called for a moratorium on new or expanded data centers within city limits until permanent regulations are established.</p><p>There are currently 39 data centers in Chicago, according to the mayor’s office. </p><p>The city’s Department of Planning and Development confirmed Thursday that since data center use is allowed under the building’s current zoning, the proposal isn’t subject to the new cross-department review that Johnson instituted in his executive order. The new review process includes an assessment of electricity demand, water use, generator impacts on noise and pollution, air emissions, cumulative environmental burdens and neighborhood effects.</p><p>Gabal told committee members there’s no industry other than data centers that can support the work needed to transform the nearly 100-year-old building. Repairs on the building’s terra cotta and “significant reinvestment” toward the building’s aging interiors are needed.</p><p>The cost of the project is unclear, but Gabal told the committee his team isn’t requesting city funding for the project. “I think it’s a win-win for everybody,” Gabal said.</p><p>Preservation Chicago was supportive of the building’s landmarking in 2009, which recognized the site as a symbol of the Loop’s transformation from industrial to office use.</p><p>But allowing the data center conversion could set a “dangerous precedent” that leads to other landmark buildings being converted to industrial use, Ward Miller, executive director of Preservation Chicago, said in the meeting.</p><p>He called for more creativity in how the office building finds its second life during a time when Chicago desperately needs more housing — especially <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/03/06/chicago-225-000-affordable-rental-units-poorest-residents-nlihc-report" >affordable</a> units.</p><p>“Preservation Chicago feels that a historic and Chicago landmark building should be adaptively used in other ways, specifically for residential reuse and not for a conversion of a Loop office building across the street from the Sears Tower, in the heart of the financial district,” Miller said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/11/mayor-brandon-johnson-chicago-moratorium-data-centers-new-regulations" >Mayor Johnson wants City Council to pause data center expansion</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: First Midway Blitz guilty plea scaled back as defendant contests account of crash with feds
entries.summary: <p>The first guilty plea tied to Operation Midway Blitz was scaled back Thursday as a Chicago man pushed back against prosecutors' claims that he’d intentionally crashed into a vehicle carrying federal officers.</p><p>In October, at the height of the Trump administration’s pummeling deportation campaign in the Chicago area, Anthony Gonzalez Alvarez joined a caravan of cars tailing a U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicle through the South Side.</p><p>Prosecutors alleged that Alvarez purposefully hit the vehicle with his truck, and he<b> </b>was charged in October with<b> </b>assaulting officers.</p><p>Alvarez then <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/15/crime-chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-ice-border-patrol" target="_blank" >pleaded guilty<b> </b>in April</a> to concealing information about a crime, a felony, admitting<b> </b>he<b> </b>falsely<b> </b>told<b> </b>the Chicago Police Department his<b> </b>Ford F-250<b> </b>had been stolen<b> </b>after<b> </b>his<b> </b>collision<b> </b>with officers. That gave the feds<b> </b>their first guilty plea<b> </b>tied to Midway Blitz.</p><p>But in June, prosecutors<b> </b>told<b> </b>U.S. District Judge<b> </b>LaShonda<b> </b>Hunt<b> </b>a<b> </b>“potential legal issue”<b> </b>had come up, and they said they’d offered<b> </b>Alvarez<b> </b>a chance<b> </b>to plead guilty<b> </b>to a misdemeanor instead.</p><p>The news came three weeks after<b> </b>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/05/26/broadview-six-andrew-boutros-kat-abughazaleh-ice-trump-chicago" target="_blank" >confirmed<b> </b>he’d spoken<b> </b>to grand jurors</a> on Oct. 23 to address “high tension”<b> </b>during Midway Blitz. That happened to be the same day grand jurors<b> </b>handed up<b> </b>an indictment<b> </b>against Alvarez.</p><p>The revelation came about because of the “Broadview Six” scandal, which revolved around <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >alleged misconduct<b> </b>by a veteran prosecutor</a> in Boutros’ office<b> </b>before grand jurors. Boutros has said “there was nothing wrong”<b> </b>with his own grand jury appearance.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure He<b> </b>waived<b> </b>indictment<b> </b>in April<b> </b>and pleaded guilty<b> </b>to a crime<b> </b>alleged<b> </b>in a separate charging document.</p><p>Now he’s withdrawn that guilty plea from April. And Thursday, Alvarez pleaded guilty again — this time to a misdemeanor count of forcibly<b> </b>interfering<b> </b>with<b> </b>federal<b> </b>officers.</p><p>Still, the downgraded charge<b> </b>is another setback for prosecutors in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >33 known nonimmigration cases</a> that were brought in relation to Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>One other defendant has pleaded guilty. Twenty-five have been cleared. Grand jurors refused to indict at least three of the 25, and another member of that group was found not guilty at trial.</p><p>In the first Midway Blitz-related sentencing last week, Hector Gomez <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/06/midway-blitz-crime-immigration-trump-hector-gomez" target="_blank" ><u>got 30 months in prison</u></a> after admitting to firing a gun near immigration agents.</p><p>In Alvarez's case, Assistant U.S. Attorney Stephanie<b> </b>Stern<b> </b>told the judge Thursday morning<b> </b>that<b> </b>three<b> </b>CBP officers<b> </b>were<b> </b>traveling<b> </b>together<b> </b>in a vehicle<b> </b>on<b> </b>Oct. 3.</p><p>Alvarez, driving his truck, joined<b> </b>a caravan<b> </b>that was following the CBP vehicle, Stern said. After<b> </b>the CBP vehicle turned<b> </b>from<b> </b>West 61st Street onto South Kedzie, she said, Alvarez drove his truck<b> </b>into the rear passenger side<b> </b>of the CBP vehicle<b> </b>in an attempt to interfere with the officers.</p><p>After hearing those allegations in court, Alvarez huddled with his attorney. He then told the judge he didn’t agree with all of Stern’s claims. He disputed that he’d driven his truck into the CBP vehicle intentionally.</p><p>“I did, in fact, hit their car. On accident,” he said. “To avoid me hitting the car in front of me that braked pretty hard.”</p><p>He added: “I dodged a car in front of me because they braked pretty hard, and that’s when I swerved toward them.”</p><p>The hearing was postponed until Thursday afternoon, when Stern presented a change in the factual basis of Alvarez’s plea.</p><p>The driver of the CBP vehicle attempted to lose the caravan, speeding up and driving into the wrong lane of traffic, Stern said. Alvarez followed the CBP vehicle, ending up in the wrong lane of traffic himself and striking the car, she said.</p><p>Alvarez agreed that everything in Stern’s revised account of the incident was true and pleaded guilty to the misdemeanor. Hunt said she’d accept the plea, pending a presentencing investigation due in October.</p><p>Alvarez’s sentencing is set for Nov. 19, and his attorney Ricardo Meza said he expects he could get up to six months' probation.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >Tracking every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s deportation blitz</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/15/crime-chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-ice-border-patrol" target="_blank" >Feds in Chicago get first guilty plea in a Midway Blitz case — but not for assaulting immigration agents</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/06/midway-blitz-crime-immigration-trump-hector-gomez" target="_blank" >30 months in prison for man who fired gun near immigration agents during Operation Midway Blitz</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: White Sox set for another big series for American League Central lead
entries.summary: <p>Another weekend, another big series in the American League Central for the first-place <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>.</p><p>Last weekend, the Guardians came to Rate Field tied for second, three games back. After the Sox took two of three, the Tigers replaced the Guardians in second place. On Friday, the Sox open a three-game series against the host Tigers, who just took two of three from the Guardians to move 2½ games back of the Sox.</p><p>“We’re really good at segmenting series,” right-hander Davis Martin said Thursday after the Sox lost two of three to the Reds at Rate Field. “We’re really good at bouncing back. There’s a reason we only have one four-loss streak. It’s a kick in the teeth, and you just pick yourself up tomorrow and do it again.”</p><p>The last time the Sox visited Detroit, they lost three straight, two by one run. The last came after they blew leads in the eighth and 10th innings.</p><p>They got a big break when the Tigers put outfielder Riley Greene on the injured list Wednesday with a strained right hamstring. He’s third on the team with 16 homers and an OPS+ of 126.</p><h3>Injured Teel ramping up</h3><p>White Sox catcher Kyle Teel is coming along quickly in his latest recovery, this time from a sprained left ankle. Venable said Teel is running at 80% speed and hopes to see him on a rehab assignment by the end of the month.</p><p>“He’s ramping up the running,” Venable said. “The hitting is going to be ahead of the running. Probably within the next couple days, he’ll take the training wheels off of everything as far as hitting, and he’ll be in there on Trajekt really getting healthy cuts off. I think the running is going to be a little bit behind.”</p><p>This is Teel’s third injury of the season. He strained his right hamstring in March during the World Baseball Classic, and while on a rehab assignment, he strained a ligament in his right knee. He made his season debut June 22, hit .191 in 19 games and injured his ankle July 20.</p><h3>McDougal makes debut</h3><p></p><p>Venable hasn’t had a problem putting rookie left-hander Hagen Smith in big spots. He had him make his major-league debut in the second inning Sunday after the rain delay, and he used him in the eighth inning Wednesday to hold a 3-0 lead.</p><p>“It just so happened that we’ve been in some tough spots and Hagen has been the best option,” Venable said.</p><p>Venable had been looking for a good spot to give rookie right-hander Tanner McDougal his first major-league appearance, and it came in the sixth inning Thursday with the Sox trailing 8-4. McDougal didn’t match Smith’s success, walking three, hitting a batter and allowing a run.</p><p>“Just couldn’t command the baseball,” Venable said. “We wasn’t able to find the zone. It just snowballed on him.”</p><p></p><h3>Thorpe could be up soon</h3><p>Right-hander Drew Thorpe, who’s on a rehab assignment after recovering from Tommy John surgery and an appendectomy, allowed one run and three hits in five innings and struck out six Wednesday in his first start at Triple-A Charlotte. Venable said Thorpe will be in the mix for a potential call-up later this month.</p><p>“I’m just really happy for him personally that he’s in a good spot and out there competing after such a tough road to get back,” Venable said. “He’s such a good guy and has worked so hard that it’s really nice to see him out there. And he’s getting good results, too. He’s pitching really well, so we’re excited about that and the opportunity to add a depth piece down the stretch.”</p><h3>On deck</h3><p><b>SOX AT TIGERS</b></p><p><b>Friday:</b> TBA vs. Jackson Jobe (1-0, 0.00 ERA), 5:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p><b>Saturday:</b> Anthony Kay (9-5, 3.96) vs. Troy Melton (7-1, 1.46), 12:10 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p><b>Sunday:</b> Sean Burke (7-6, 2.99) vs. Drew entries.title: Some Lake View residents worry about more booms as Thunderbirds return to Air and Water Show
entries.summary: <p>One year after the Air Force Thunderbirds sent two suspected sonic booms rippling across Chicago, some Lake View residents say they are concerned about more possible blasts at this weekend's Air and Water Show.</p><p>Lakefront residents told the Sun-Times they remember hearing the booms during last year's Friday practice run that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/08/15/lakeview-apartment-windows-shatter-from-jets-practicing-for-air-and-water-show" target="_blank" >shattered the windows</a> of four lakefront high-rises. </p><p>“When the sonic boom hit, the whole building shook,” Claire Falk, who lives in a high-rise in Lake View, told a Sun-Times reporter during a stroll through the neighborhood Thursday.</p><p>The Air Force denied the loud booms, which were captured last year on several videos, were the planes going supersonic. But one aeronautics experts told the Sun-Times that the videos <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/08/18/sonic-booms-lake-view-thunderbirds-chicago-air-water-show" target="_blank" >clearly showed that they were</a>.</p><p>Dennis Straight, who lives in a high-rise near Lake Shore Drive and Belmont Avenue and remembers reports of the damage, plans to watch this year's Air and Water Show, which is set for Saturday and Sunday, centered at North Avenue Beach. </p><p>He said he hopes officials take steps to prevent another incident — and that the pilots watch their speeds a little more closely this time.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-700000" "It's just, like, slow it down a little bit.”</p><p>Straight also said he would like to see more communication from officials about what residents should expect.</p><p>“It'd be nice if they'd say that. People are worried about it,” he said.</p><p>Local Ald. Bennett Lawson (44th) gave the Sun-Times a statement: “The Air & Water Show is a longstanding Chicago tradition, but the safety of our residents and their property must come first. Following reports of property damage in Lakeview during last year’s rehearsal, I joined neighboring alderpersons in raising concerns with the City and requesting additional safeguards to prevent similar incidents.”</p><p>“As this year’s show approaches, our office continues to expect the City and its partners to take appropriate precautions to ensure the event can be enjoyed safely and responsibly," Lawson said.</p><p>Last year, Lawson said the damage was limited to the first floors of four condo buildings in the 3180, 3600 and 3950 blocks of North Lake Shore Drive and 4200 N. Marine Drive. At the time, he encouraged the building owners to file claims with the city to be reimbursed for the damage.</p><p>The Thunderbirds and city's Office of Emergency Management and Communications, which coordinates public safety at the Air and Water Show, did not reply to the Sun-Times request for comment on what safety precautions are being taken this year.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Bears need to play QB Caleb Williams at some point this preseason to check his progress
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson’s confidence is contagious, and he has a lot of credibility in the bank after an excellent first season, so it’s easy to buy into any plan he makes. If he says quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> is good to go for the season, who’s going to question that?</p><p>But as eager as everyone seems to be to proclaim Williams’ arrival, he’s not at that point yet.</p><p>It’s reasonable that Johnson will hold him out of the preseason opener Saturday against the Browns, but when he delivered that news Thursday, he floated the possibility that Williams could skip the entire preseason schedule.</p><p>“Do I need to see Caleb Williams in the preseason? No, I don't,” Johnson said before practice. “I see him every single day in practice and I know what we're going to get come the season.”</p><p>Instead, Johnson explained how he’s using guidance from the training staff about how much of a workload players should have. He might opt to get Williams those snaps exclusively in practice, especially in the upcoming joint practices with the Bengals and Titans, but said it’s “really, really fluid on how we’re handling that” and he could allot some of that work to the preseason games against those teams.</p><p>He has a plan, for example, of how many snaps he wants Williams to take next week over the course of three practices at Halas Hall, one in Cincinnati and the Aug. 22 preseason game, but hasn’t divided them up yet.</p><p>Given that the Bears remain unsettled at left tackle — Kiran Amegadjie and Jedrick Wills will share time Saturday with Braxton Jones recovering from a knee injury — and wouldn’t have much inclination to play a veteran like left guard Joe Thuney in preseason games, it’s prudent to hold Williams out of this one.</p><p>So backup Tyson Bagent will start Saturday and likely play the first half, then Johnson has third-stringer Case Keenum and undrafted rookie Miller Moss available for the second.</p><p>But at some point, there needs to be a live-action check of Williams' progress.</p><p>When established quarterbacks like Jared Goff and Josh Allen skip the preseason, they have definitive bodies of work to justify it. Williams made incredible plays last season and led some stunning comebacks, but he’s very much a work-in-progress.</p><p>And Johnson, by the way, has been saying some version of that all offseason. He loves the highlights, but he wants more precision, more fluency in the offense and more anticipation of how defenders will react.</p><p>Johnson should want some concrete confirmation that what he’s seen in practice will be there in games. It’s true that Williams is further along than he was a year ago, when Johnson sat him in the preseason opener but played him significantly in the next two games, but the Bears’ offense has had some hiccups even at Halas Hall.</p><p>Johnson won’t get a complete assessment, including Williams’ ability to meet his requirement of completing 70% of his passes, until the real games. He would, however, get a good look at whether Williams is running pre-snap maneuvers proficiently and keeping the offense organized.</p><p>That was an issue last preseason. It appeared things were smoothing out somewhat, then Johnson was surprised by the Bears’ string of debacles in their finale against the Chiefs.</p><p>“It is disappointing to me offensively, for sure, because I thought that we’d kind of worked our way out of that,” Johnson said that night at Arrowhead Stadium.</p><p>He doesn’t want to feel that way in Week 1 against the Panthers, does he?</p><p>It’s likely that Johnson wants to reveal as little as possible to the rest of the NFL about updates to his offense and improvements by Williams, but that’s going to be evident soon enough anyway. After that Sept. 13 opener, nobody will be caught off-guard by what the Bears are running.</p><p>The real issue Johnson is weighing is whether getting a status report on Williams and the offense is worth risking an injury in a preseason game.</p><p>The Bears already have had some injuries in training camp, including a possible season-ender for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/11/bears-s-coby-bryant-undergoes-knee-surgery-now-out-until-at-least-december" >safety Coby Bryant,</a> but quarterback is the one position that coaches can almost guarantee protection because defenders aren’t allowed to touch them in practice.</p><p>Williams made so many memorable plays last season that they overshadowed how much work still lies ahead.</p><p>His touchdown pass late in the playoff game against the Rams might’ve been the best play of the NFL season. It seems to slip some minds that the Bears actually lost that game on an interception because of a miscommunication between Williams and DJ Moore and that Williams completed 22 of 41 passes other than that fourth-and-eight heave to Cole Kmet.</p><p>The Bears scored only 17 points that night, one of their worst performances of the season offensively.</p><p>For all the progress behind the scenes, that’s the last time anyone has seen the offense or Williams in a game. It’s not a good idea to go into the regular season eight months later without taking at least a quick look at where they stand.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module entries.title: Tras seis meses detenida por ICE, una vendedora de tamales de Chicago reconstruye su vida
entries.summary: <p>A través de la ventana de un vehículo del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) mientras se alejaba el pasado septiembre, Laura Murillo pudo ver su puesto de tamales cerca del concurrido Home Depot ubicado en 47th Street y Western Avenue. Una mesa plegable sostenía hieleras, recipientes y suministros bajo una sombrilla de rayas junto a su minivan plateada. Sólo minutos antes, Murillo, una inmigrante de México, había estado esperando a sus clientes.</p><p>La noche antes de su detención, Murillo había preparado los tamales en la cocina de un edificio de ladrillo que alquilaba en el lado sureste. Antes del amanecer, ella y una trabajadora los empacaron en su camioneta y ella condujo para instalar su puesto.</p><p>Durante años, Murillo organizó gran parte de su vida en torno a esta rutina. El negocio de los tamales le permitió a la madre de dos hijas mantenerse, sostener a sus niñas y ofrecer trabajo a otras mujeres. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b20000" name="module-b20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Aunque era un trabajo agotador, era central para la forma en que Murillo se entendía a sí misma: como proveedora independiente, dueña de un negocio y alguien en quien los demás podían confiar.</p><p>"Todo era trabajo", dice Murillo, con la confianza de quien está acostumbrada a manejar las cosas por su cuenta. "Era felicidad".</p><p>Pero la mujer de 55 años ahora cuestiona la vida que había construido en torno al trabajo constante. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/27/tamale-vendor-arrested-back-of-the-yards-ice-immigration" target="_blank" >Fue detenida</a> durante el Operativo Midway Blitz, la agresiva campaña de deportaciones ocurrida el otoño pasado, y pasó seis meses en detención migratoria federal.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Día a día, ya", cuenta Murillo.</p><h3>El trabajo del cuidado</h3><p>Murillo llegó por primera vez a Chicago en 2005 desde Tamaulipas, México, con su entonces pareja, esperando quedarse sólo unos años. En lugar de eso, consiguieron trabajo, criaron a sus hijas, Génesis, ahora de 20 años, y Daniela, de 17, y construyeron una vida en la ciudad.</p><p>La joven madre trabajó primero en fábricas antes de aprender el oficio de los tamales.</p><p>En 2013, su amiga cercana Gina Otamendi se había separado de su esposo y criaba a cuatro niños pequeños cuando acudió a Murillo en busca de trabajo.</p><p>Murillo la contrató, le enseñó a hacer y vender tamales y organizó sus horarios en función del horario escolar de los niños, dándole a Otamendi la flexibilidad que necesitaba como madre soltera.</p><p>"Me dejaba salir a darle de comer a mis hijos y llevarlos a la escuela porque tenia que trabajar para yo poder pagar todo lo que se necesitaban", cuenta Otamendi. "Me daba de comer. Siempre me ayudó".</p><p>Otamendi, de 50 años, recuerda largas jornadas haciendo tamales, pero también música y risas. Las mujeres competían para ver quién hacía más tamales en una hora. Cantaban y bailaban mientras trabajaban.</p><p>"[Fue] una amistad muy bonita", dice Otamendi.</p><p>Años después, Otamendi ayudaría a las hijas de Murillo mientras su madre estaba detenida.</p><p>Otamendi revisaba cómo estaban Génesis y Daniela, llevaba comestibles y organizaba las comidas.</p><p>También puso en contacto a la familia con el Centro de Trabajadores Unidos, También se convirtió en el contacto principal con el abogado que llevaba el caso de su mamá.</p><p>"Actualmente soy estudiante universitaria a tiempo completo haciendo lo posible por mantener todo, pero mi sueldo no alcanza para todos los gastos legales y del hogar que han surgido de repente", escribió Génesis en una página de GoFundMe en septiembre de 2025.</p><p>"Yo hablaba con ella", dice Otamendi. "Y pobrecita, se desesperaba y decía: Gina, ¿cómo le voy a hacer?’"</p><p>Daniela, a quien Murillo describe como con necesidades especiales, aprendió a lavar los platos, sacar la basura y encargarse mejor de su cuidado personal.</p><p>La comunidad también intervino. La mañana después de que Murillo fuera detenida, vecinos y organizadores <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/27/tamale-vendor-arrested-back-of-the-yards-ice-immigration" target="_blank" >ocuparon su lugar habitual</a>, vendiendo más de 300 tamales en cerca de una hora para recaudar dinero para su familia.</p><h3>Dentro de la detención</h3><p>Murillo estuvo a casi 1,500 millas de distancia, en Camp East Montana en El Paso, Texas.</p><p>Allí conoció a mujeres cuya vida afuera empezaba a desmoronarse.</p><p>Había mujeres mayores cuyos esposos habían dejado de contestarles. Algunas decían que sus hijos ya no les mandaban dinero. Había madres separadas de sus familias, una mujer que caminaba con un bastón y otra que usaba silla de ruedas.</p><p>Una mujer, recordó Murillo, había sido arrestada mientras regaba el patio fuera de su casa.</p><p>"¿Qué crímenes supuestamente cometieron?", sigue preguntando Murillo. "Estaban en sus casas".</p><p>Los oficiales de inmigración le pidieron a Murillo en dos ocasiones que firmara papeles de salida voluntaria, pero ella se negó y esperó mientras sus abogados impugnaban su detención.</p><p>Otras mujeres terminaron firmando, dice, porque se habían desesperado y ya no creían que nadie las ayudara.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Dice que su fe la ayudó a soportar la incertidumbre y lo que ella describe como un abuso psicológico por parte de los guardias. Una mujer de un refugio católico cercano la visitó y leyó pasajes de la Biblia.</p><p>Los guardias, mientras tanto, con frecuencia les recordaban a las mujeres lo poco que podían controlar, cuenta.</p><p>Cuando Murillo preguntaba la hora, decía que la cuestionaban sobre por qué necesitaba saberla. Cuando quería calcetines limpios, dice que uno le respondió, "¿Para qué? No vas a salir".</p><p>Incapaz de desempeñar el papel que había desempeñado durante tanto tiempo en casa, Murillo solo pudo hablar con sus hijas por teléfono.</p><p>"Lo que más extrañaba eran las caritas de mis hijas", dice Murillo.</p><p>"Cuando te encierran, pierdes el control. [Mis hijas] ya no me llamaban para preguntarme cosas ni pedir permiso. Mis hijas estaban haciendo las cosas por su cuenta".</p><p>Para la primavera pasada, no tenía muchas esperanzas de ser liberada. Pero a finales de marzo, el gobierno federal liberó inesperadamente a Murillo después de reconocer que su arresto había violado el <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/27/judge-orders-32-detainees-released-over-ice-consent-decree-violations-unclear-how-many-still-in-custody" target="_blank" >acuerdo de consentimiento Castañón Nava</a>, un arreglo de 2022 de la corte federal que limitaba las detenciones migratorias sin órdenes.</p><p>Una vez liberada, los oficiales llevaron a Murillo a un refugio católico en El Paso, donde pasó el fin de semana. Murillo dice que le tomó tiempo entender que estaba libre. Inicialmente permaneció dentro del refugio hasta que una mujer allí le recordó que podía salir. Murillo dio un paseo y asistió a misa la mañana siguiente.</p><p>Sus hijas habían planeado visitarla en detención, y decidieron hacer el viaje de todas formas para traer a su madre a casa. Llegaron ese domingo y volaron de regreso con ella a Chicago.</p><p>"Cuando pasan en las películas que salen de un proceso y llegan y besan el piso, casi yo quería hacer eso.", dice Murillo. "Te lo juro, de verdad lo viví así".</p><h3>Una vida distinta en Chicago</h3><p>De vuelta en casa, Murillo no quiere reconstruir la misma vida, pero sabe que todavía necesita —y quiere— trabajar.</p><p>Ha pensado en abrir una pequeña tamalería sin el horario tan exigente que antes llevaba. Murillo muestra sus manos, enseñando la artritis reumatoide que dice tener por moverse repetidamente entre el calor y el frío al cocinar y vender tamales durante los inviernos de Chicago.</p><p>"Ya no veo la vida como a querer matarme tratando por querer lograr cosas", dice Murillo. "Ya no".</p><p>La renuencia de Murillo a retomar su antiguo ritmo y rutina refleja un retraimiento similar entre otros vendedores ambulantes.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </figure> </div> </div><p>Casi un año después del inicio del Operativo Midway Blitz, líderes de la Asociación de Vendedores Ambulantes de Chicago dijeron que el miedo continúa determinando cuándo —y si— los vendedores salen a ofrecer sus productos.</p><p>Los vendedores que siguen trabajando aún corren el riesgo de control migratorio, incluso cuando <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/07/10/los-arrestos-de-ice-han-aumentado-en-chicago-pero-con-tacticas-menos-llamativas-que-el-otono-pasado" target="_blank" >los agentes de ICE han realizado arrestos de forma más discreta</a> que durante el punto más alto de la campaña de deportaciones del presidente Donald Trump. Los líderes de la asociación también dijeron que agentes de policía locales han aumentado la vigilancia sobre los vendedores ambulantes por vender sin licencias o en áreas prohibidas.</p><p>Murillo dice que está en proceso de obtener su estatus legal. No se sintió cómoda al compartir detalles debido a su reciente detención. Su pareja ayuda con la renta. Génesis empezó a pagar su propio teléfono e internet.</p><p>Murillo se siente orgullosa de sus hijas, aunque admite que fue difícil aceptar que ellas habían aprendido a manejar mucho más por su cuenta.</p><p>"Estoy batallando un poquito", dice Murillo. "Como que ya no me necesitaron".</p><p>Murillo pasa más tiempo con ellas, incluidos paseos al parque y al cine. Durante años, el trabajo venía primero. "Espera hasta mañana, espera hasta mañana", recuerda que les decía cuando querían pasar tiempo juntas.</p><p>Después de haber definido durante mucho tiempo la independencia como poder cuidarse a sí misma y a los demás sin pedir ayuda, Murillo ahora entiende cuánta gente intervino mientras ella estuvo ausente, trayendo comida, ofreciendo dinero, consejos y ayudando a sus hijas a sobrellevar los meses sin ella.</p><p>"Mami, no tienes idea como la gente te quiere", recuerda Murillo que le dijo Génesis. "Ni siquiera te imaginas".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Broadway Antique Market, Chicago's largest multi-dealer antique store, up for sale
entries.summary: <p>After nearly 30 years in Edgewater, the owners of Broadway Antique Market are retiring and selling the store. </p><p>Co-owners Duane Scott Cerny and Jeff Nelson have run the city's largest and oldest multi-dealer antique store, at 6130 N. Broadway, since 1998, when they moved their business from Wrigleyville.</p><p>"We have contributed to the decor of literally thousands of homes around the country," Cerny, 67, told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Part of their motivation to sell is their ballooning annual property tax bill, which recently spiked to $103,000 from $70,000, Cerny said.</p><p>"A six-figure bill is just not sustainable," he said.</p><p>Property taxes aside, business has been solid for a long time, Cerny said, adding that he has watched Edgewater thrive since moving to the neighborhood. He is excited about recent efforts to redevelopment Broadway for more growth.</p><p>"The neighborhood has been good to us," Cerny said. "Ideally, what we're hoping is for someone to come in who can buy the business and the building and keep the store alive." </p><p>Cerny and Nelson don't have an official last day yet. The store will stay open through the winter holidays.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" href="https://www.loopnet.com/Listing/6130-N-Broadway-St-Chicago-IL/41465317/" target="_blank" >listed for $2.5 million</a>. It was built in 1939 as a furniture store. When Cerny and Nelson bought the building, they saved it from becoming a Blockbuster Video store. Before that, they ran an antique store in Wrigleyville for eight years.</p><p>Some of the dealers at the Broadway Antique Market have had stalls at the store since the Wrigleyville days. Many plan to retire alongside Cerny and Nelson.</p><p> </p><p>One of them is Jeff Cohen of Lincoln Park, who started selling at the Cerny and Nelson's first antique mall in 1990. He happily followed them to the Edgewater store and remains a vendor today.</p><p>"We have had a long run. It's been terrific," Cohen said. "If Broadway closes, that’ll be my calling to retire." </p><p>Cohen sells jewelry, vintage watches and Art Deco home decor. He said it will be a sad day if the shop closes. </p><p>Chicago has many vintage and antique stores, he said, but the multi-dealer-style shop at Broadway Antique Market is a dying breed.</p><p>"It's a destination for Chicagoans — for tourists, for bargain shoppers, for collectors, for other antique sellers," Cohen said. "It's not just an antique mall. What they've built is a department store of cool and unique finds."</p><p>Cerny said he is ready to retire and devote more of his energy to writing. In 2018, he published a memoir about being an antique dealer, "Selling Dead People’s Things." He also writes a column for The Village View, a New York City newspaper.</p><p>Their store is loved by local residents and international visitors, Cerny said. Broadway Antique Market is listed in an Italian guidebook as one of the top 10 things to do in Chicago — alongside the Art Institute and Magnificent Mile.</p><p>"I just want to give a huge thank you to Chicago for putting us on the map," Cerny said.</p>
